articles.title_orig: Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
articles.content_orig:
U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve .
Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S.
This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in.
"They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning."
The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history.
The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s.
Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s .
Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week.
One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy.
Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock.
All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth.
"Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank."
At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures.
During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment.
At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched.
Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest rates in September , Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027.
In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs.
"Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize."
In Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills.
Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation. Adding to their woes is the fact that year-over-year inflation has run at a faster clip than wage growth in recent months, meaning the average consumer has lost purchasing power.
The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment survey earlier this year fell to the lowest levels ever seen . The highest share of respondents citing high prices as a reason for having worse personal finances surpassed 50% for the first time on record in 2026.
High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."
Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and President Donald Trump in the midterm election.
Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.
Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.
Olena Nicks, an analyst and local lawmaker in Long Island, New York, is one of those consumers tightening the purse strings in the face of lofty prices. Nicks said she's specifically noticed steep price increases over recent years in the grocery store produce aisle and when looking at airline flights for vacations.
In response, the 34-year-old said she's cut back on purchasing meals at restaurants or from fast-food chains. Her friend group has forgone leisure activities like bowling, opting instead for less-costly nights spent in someone's home.
"Frustrated is an understatement," Nicks said. "It feels like you're stuck."

articles.title_orig: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.title_zh: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.content_orig:
Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online
A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago , as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.
The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.
In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.
She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.
A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.
The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.
No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.
Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.
“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.
“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”
The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.
Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.
Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks sink two ships in Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks sink two ships in Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.
The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore .
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.
Containers were floating in the water after the vessel sank, Pakistani maritime authorities warned in a navigational alert . It is the third commercial ship sunk during the Iran war, according to the International Maritime Organization , a United Nations' agency.
A second Singapore-registered container ship, the GFS Giselle, sustained damage to its hull after it was hit by an unidentified projectile on Wednesday. The ship has arrived at safe anchorage and none of its crew were hurt, the Singapore maritime authority said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to the state news agency Tasnim . But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks.
Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert.
Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait.
More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and more than a dozen injured, according to the IMO.
Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased. Oil prices closed slightly higher Wednesday.
Exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler .
Shipments from the Middle East, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed.
Daily crude flows are very volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

articles.title_orig: The Trump-Xi Summit Exposed the Problems in China-US Crisis Management - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The Trump-Xi Summit Exposed the Problems in China-US Crisis Management - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump salutes during the playing of the U.S. national anthem at a welcome ceremony for Chinese President Xi Jinping (left), Sep. 23, 2026.
Xi Jinping’s September visit to Washington ended without a major breakthrough on trade or artificial intelligence safety. Most media coverage focused on the ceremony and the limited results. The official accounts, however, raised important questions about crisis management, which has gone largely undiscussed.
China’s readout said the two militaries had “agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding as soon as possible on strengthening crisis communication and prevention.” The White House “fact sheet ” did not mention that commitment. A later South China Morning Post report said a U.S. official denied that the discussion had taken place.
Before any MoU can improve crisis management, Washington and Beijing first need a consensus that they agreed to pursue such a mechanism.
China and the United States already have several ways to communicate during military tensions. These include the Defense Telephone Link , direct contact between their leaders, and regular meetings between defense officials. They have also agreed on rules for military encounters at sea and in the air .
Yet having these arrangements in place does not mean they will be used when a crisis occurs. Officials may delay answering a call, and political tensions might lead either government to suspend talks altogether. The proposed memorandum should therefore focus on keeping existing contacts available when they are most needed.
For more than a year after then-U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s August 2022 visit to Taiwan, senior U.S. and Chinese military officers had few opportunities to speak directly. Beijing had canceled talks between theater commanders and suspended other defense meetings in protest against the visit. The military contacts themselves were not the source of the disagreement, but they became part of Beijing’s response.
Presidents Xi Jinping and Joe Biden eventually agreed to resume military talks when they met in California in November 2023, and the U.S. Department of Defense welcomed the move. But restoring contact after a leaders’ meeting is one thing; making sure those channels remain open when relations are strained is another.
The current Defense Telephone Link is not designed for situations that require an immediate response. According to the International Crisis Group , arranging a call normally involves giving 48 hours’ notice, and the other side has another 24 hours to respond to the request. Senior officials may be able to work with these rules when arranging meetings in advance. An emergency – say, an aircraft collision in the South China Sea – would leave little time for such procedures. By the time a call was arranged, commanders might already have made decisions without hearing from their counterparts.
The 2001 EP-3 collision offers another example of how difficult communication can be during a military crisis. The U.S. embassy tried to contact Chinese officials after the collision between U.S. and Chinese military aircraft, but received few answers during the first 12 hours. Washington had little information about how Beijing was handling the incident.
The Defense Telephone Link had not yet been established in 2001, making the circumstances different from today. But recent precedent is not encouraging either. In early 2023, after the U.S. military shot down a Chinese surveillance balloon that had overflown the U.S. mainland, the U.S. defense secretary tried to arrange a call with his Chinese counterpart. China reportedly rejected his request for contact.
That episode underscored the limited value of existing crisis management mechanisms. When urgent calls go unanswered, military officers have to make decisions with limited information about the other side’s intentions.
The proposed crisis management MoU needs to handle these two problems. Even if regular military talks break down, both sides should still be able to reach each other in an emergency. It should also require an acknowledgment within 30 minutes of an urgent message being sent. The officer receiving the message would simply confirm that it had arrived and that the information was being checked. Neither side would have to admit fault or agree with the other’s account at this stage. They could leave those disagreements for later, once the immediate risk had been dealt with.
For Beijing, accepting a message is different from deciding how to respond to it. Chinese officers may have to consult their superiors before commenting on an incident, particularly one involving sovereignty or military activity. That process can take time. A simple reply verifying receipt would allow those discussions to continue without leaving Washington unsure whether its warning had been heard. Beijing could still decide what to say after reviewing the incident, while keeping the military line open during the most urgent stage of a crisis.
The International Crisis Group has called for crisis simulations in which Chinese and American officials examine how each side might respond as tensions develop. A hypothetical aircraft collision over the South China Sea would be a useful scenario for a joint exercise before the November Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The U.S. military could make the initial test call and wait for a response from its Chinese counterpart, following the same procedures that would apply in a real incident. The exercise would give both sides a chance to see how long a message takes to reach the officer responsible for answering it. Any delay caused by the need to seek approval would become apparent.
An emergency channel should focus on what is happening at the time of a crisis. If an incident occurs, both sides need to know where it happened, whether anyone was injured, and whether their forces might come into contact again. They should not have to settle wider disagreements before sharing such information. Questions over Taiwan, technology restrictions, and U.S. military deployments can still be discussed through existing diplomatic and defense channels. Keeping these issues out of emergency communication would allow officers to deal with the immediate situation without waiting for progress in political negotiations.
Xi’s remarks in Washington called for the Chinese and U.S. militaries to “maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” Leader-level diplomacy can authorize this work, but that doesn’t guarantee progress. By the next Trump-Xi summit at APEC, both governments should at least confirm the same commitment and complete a test of the contact route. The MoU itself may take longer if the two sides are still negotiating its terms.
The leader-level summits will matter more if the two governments can agree on how to handle calls during a military crisis. In the past, political disputes have led Beijing to suspend military exchanges with Washington. The same problem could arise again, leaving officers unable to contact their counterparts at a critical moment. One way to prevent this would be to keep emergency hotlines separate from regular defense talks. The first measure of progress is therefore simple: whether both militaries can agree that an urgent message must be acknowledged within 30 minutes.

articles.title_orig: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
articles.title_zh: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
articles.content_orig:
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".
Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures.
Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show.
With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.
As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.
Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.
In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.
The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.
Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.
Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."
Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.
So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.
On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.
Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.
Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.
He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."
And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.
Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report at the start of this year.
Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.
The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.
Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.
From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.
Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.
Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.
Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.
Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.
This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.
This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.
"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.
The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.
That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.
"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.
If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.
While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.
Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud
US politics live – latest updates
Federal authorities investigating the Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities investigate potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington DC home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms , in which Omar is seeking re-election.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also looking into issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests, which will determine control of the House and the Senate, was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the representative for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”.
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.

Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

articles.title_orig: Mary Cassatt exhibit at Art Institute aims to recreate lost mural from 1893 World's Fair
articles.title_zh: Mary Cassatt exhibit at Art Institute aims to recreate lost mural from 1893 World's Fair
articles.content_orig:
The 1893 World's Fair looms large in Chicago history.
Now, one of its groundbreaking works of art is a centerpiece of a new exhibit at the Art Institute of Chicago — but there is one big problem.
At the heart of this exhibit at the Art Institute is a work that no longer exists.
"It's a tough problem for a curator to have, to center this story about a monumental mural without the mural," said Annelise Madsen with the Art Institute.
That mural, " Modern Woman " by Mary Cassatt, was from the 1893 World's Fair.
"It was Cassatt really scaling up her subject matter, what she had built her career portraying, the lives of everyday women, but giving that a sense of import, a sense of grandeur," Madsen said.
Cassatt now has her own exhibit at the Art Institute, which aims to recreate the form and spirit of the long-lost mural.
"What we do have are a lot of enticing traces," Madsen said. "We have archival material. We have reproductions of the mural that are in fair publications from the 1890s. We have letters by Cassatt."
The exhibit covers a lifetime of Cassatt's work beyond the missing mural — like the iconic painting, "The Child's Bath," from 1893.
"She was a fierce, independent woman and an artist of the time," Madsen said. "I think she was, first of all, showing us the impact of human connection."
Her impact still felt, even through a mural that we can't see.
"It's a Chicago story, and we, for that reason alone, we must embrace it. It's part of the history of this city."
Mary Cassatt actually helped the art institute get one of its signature works — El Greco's " The Assumption of the Virgin ."
In 1905, Cassatt wrote to the institute's president when the painting became available, saying it belonged there.
Cassatt's exhibit runs through January 3, 2027.

Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) Q3 revenue climbed to $16.8 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the second quarter.
The AI startup revealed the news to investors during a closed meeting, noting that it is also profitable on an adjusted basis, according to The Financial Times .
The news comes as Wall Street awaits Anthropic's public S-1 filing. The company p rivately filed the paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1.
Anthropic is projected to kick off its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) sometime this fall, with the Street eyeing a record $2 trillion valuation.
The latest revenue numbers come after the Financial Tim es reported that investors revised their estimates for Anthropic rival OpenAI's annualized revenue downward from $70 billion to $50 billion .
Investors, the report says, initially miscalculated OpenAI's numbers while attempting to match them to Anthropic's revenue run rate, resulting in a massive $20 billion swing.
While Anthropic is ramping up for its IPO, OpenAI is holding off on its until early 2027. According to Bloomberg , the company is instead looking to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation.
The two AI companies, as well as Meta ( META ) and Google ( GOOG ), have faced mounting pressure in recent months after reporting that their respective AI models broke free of containment and hacked into third-party websites and networks.
That's led to increased calls for regulations around AI models and their use. But President Trump has pushed back, opting for self-regulation among the companies.
Earlier this month, Trump convened a meeting of leading AI executives, including Amodei, at which they signed what Trump called a "morally binding" agreement to have independent auditors review their models for suspicious behavior.
Anthropic and OpenAI are also contending with a growing pricing war among AI model makers. With "tokenmaxxing" in the rearview, AI customers are looking for ways to save on AI expenses, whether that's through open-weight models from China or less expensive closed models from leading US labs.
Last week, Anthropic debuted its Claude Haiku 5.5 , saying it costs an average of 75% less than Haiku 4.5. Customers pay $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per output token. That's in line with rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) smallest model, GPT-6 Luna.
Tokens are a measure of AI usage and represent portions of or entire words users type into prompt boxes and the responses the AI spits back out.

articles.title_orig: Ancient shipwreck discovered off Turkey claimed to be world’s oldest
articles.title_zh: Ancient shipwreck discovered off Turkey claimed to be world’s oldest
articles.content_orig:
Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova Island
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.
They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.
The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.
The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Ãniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.
The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages
The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope,  just 30m beneath the waves.
Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.
The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.
Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.
The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.
Ãniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.
"Comparing the decoration techniquesâ¦ we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."
The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship
After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved
Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.
Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spotsâ¦. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.
"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.
"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."
The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.
The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.
The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts
Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.
There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.
Ãniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.
"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.
The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it
The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.
Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.
The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

articles.title_orig: Measles cases surge past 150 in Kentucky; big outbreak identified in one county
articles.title_zh: Measles cases surge past 150 in Kentucky; big outbreak identified in one county
articles.content_orig:
Just days after Kentucky's measles case count hit 100, dozens more have been reported.
As of Wednesday, the number of cases reported in the Commonwealth is now 157 for 2026.
Most of those come out of Laurel County, which had seven cases just a few days ago. Now, it has 56, according to the state's dashboard .
Laurel County is in southeast Kentucky,
The dashboard says that outbreak involves people who are unvaccinated from several large households that have been "isolated from the broader community."
In only one case did the person report having the full vaccine. One case had one MMR dose, and the rest didn't have any.
Of the total state count, nine of those cases have led to hospitalization.
So far, no deaths have been reported.
There were only 13 cases overall in 2025, and none were reported the year prior.
Measles is a disease caused by a highly contagious virus.
It is spread through the air when someone with measles sneezes, coughs, or breathes.
Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes, and rash. Tiny white spots can appear inside the mouth two to three days after symptoms begin.
The disease can be especially severe in infants, pregnant women, and people who have weakened immune systems.
While rare, measles can result in death.
Kentucky health officials have warned this is the highest case count in decades. Dr. Steve Stack, with the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, along with other local health officials, has been encouraging people to get vaccinated.
"We do not need to have measles," Gov. Andy Beshear said last month. "We have a proven tool that for over a quarter century eliminated it from the United States. The only reason it's resurging now is because of, I think, negligent information and guidance being shared freely. We want people to not feel vilified or maligned. We want people to feel informed."

articles.title_orig: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
articles.title_zh: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Football coaches have the freedom to create their own worlds on the playing field. But retired Steelers legend Mike Tomlin took a different route — manifesting his vision block by block within a massive Minecraft city. What started as a shared family project with his children evolved into a solitary, 12-year labor of love. Now, the sheer depth of Tomlin’s digital city is capturing widespread attention online.
Tomlin served as the Steelers’ head coach for 19 seasons before resigning in January, having never finished with a losing record.
His video was released Oct. 1 and received more than 3 million views in less than two weeks. In the video, Tomlin shows off an expansive Minecraft city, complete with sports stadiums, high-rise apartments, homes and other buildings. He began working on the city about 12 years ago after watching his kids and their friends play Minecraft when they were in middle school, building it in the game’s creative mode with their help.
“I was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin says in the video. “I’m certainly not skilled enough in video game play or have the stick control to [play the game’s survival mode], so I got interested in this creative mode. I like to build, I’ve always had an interest in architecture, and so I started doing this creative city as a means to spend time with them.”
His kids eventually outgrew the game and moved on to different ones, high school and eventually college. That left Tomlin to work on the city by himself, which he did off and on for years while still coaching the Steelers.
“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me, some mindless entertainment,” Tomlin says. “I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life.”
Tomlin spends the rest of the video showing viewers around the place, focusing on his basic, early-days architecture, penthouses, apartments and how he tried to design a solid urban space. He plans to release more videos to discuss different buildings, the city’s design and other elements of his sprawling city.
Leading up to the video’s release, there was no indication whatsoever that Mike Tomlin played computer games. That helped make his big Minecraft debut all the more delightful. The 54-year-old coach showed off thousands of hours of playtime in a 19-minute video, and no one could believe it.
“12 years of Minecraft? Didn’t you know this? Did nobody know this?” asked a shocked Ty Schmidt, producer and on-air personality of the Pat McAfee show, on an episode of the show.
The sports world finally saw what some Minecraft fans already knew: Tomlin’s dedication to the game is unmatched.
“We’re talking block by block,” McAfee said. “He had 14 30-story buildings around a body of water that he wanted to build his city around — one block at a time! They all got patios! He had a penthouse with a shark aquarium. It was unbelievable.”
Minecraft fans, too, showed up to explore the coach’s dazzling feat. Many were surprised to learn that he built this on the Bedrock edition of the game using a video game console, beginning with PlayStation 3 before moving on to PlayStation 4 and 5. That means Tomlin didn’t have access to the mods that many builders use in the Java version of the game on PC, or the freedom that a mouse and keyboard provide. He built his city one brick at a time on a PlayStation controller.
Tomlin was initially unaware of his viral fame. In an interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Tomlin said he was at a gala with his phone off when the video went live, and it wasn’t until later that his kids told him about the massive response. Tomlin had caught up by the time he appeared on Football Night in America with NBC on Sunday night.
“I’m appreciating all of this, to be quite honest with you,” Tomlin said during the broadcast.
The spectacle of Tomlin’s Minecraft city is one of those wholesome events that had viewers smiling all weekend, except a few Steelers fans who were probably already pretty mad about losing to the Cleveland Browns less than 24 hours after the video was released. That didn’t stop a lot of people from wondering whether Tomlin’s city is actually as good as it looks. It turns out that most of the Internet agrees that it lives up to the hype.
“From my understanding, [it’s a] phenomenal Minecraft city,” McAfee said. “Like, as I was watching it, I was like, man, the attention to detail [is outstanding].”
Noted Minecraft city builder Alpine1 was one of the first to create his own video on the topic, and he was impressed. He had some suggestions for Tomlin, recommending that the coach consider using glass panes instead of glass blocks and more sophisticated floor designs, such as installing tile floors in showers. But Alpine1 did note that Tomlin likely started building the city before many modern building tools were available to Minecraft players.
“This is really awesome to see,” Alpine1 said in the video. “I’ve been advocating for people to build Minecraft cities for years because there’s so much you can do… and I think Mike has really captured this.”
Zach Nagel, an architecture student from the University of Cincinnati’s School of Architecture and Interior Design, also took a stab at analyzing Tomlin’s city in a separate video . He noted that Tomlin used some concepts that are actually practiced in architecture, specifically adding a penthouse with an aquarium right across the street from a full-sized aquarium.
“Now, what Coach Tomlin is talking about here, having a central theme to the building, is a term that we use in architecture as well, the parti ,” Nagel says. “If you talk to 20 architects and ask them to give a definition of a parti, you might get 20 pretty different answers. At its [simplest], a parti is a single idea or scheme that drives all of the decisions you make in a building.”
Nagel goes on to praise Tomlin for not only considering the building’s exterior appearance but also its interior design and the functional needs of the city’s fictional residents. He says that a lot of Tomlin’s design choices and approach are in line with what some architects use.
“In another world, he could’ve totally gone down this career path had he wanted to,” Nagel says. “And I’m glad to see that Minecraft remains such an accessible tool for those who want to shape the environment around them.”

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court Again Sides With Republicans in Political TV Ad Fight
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court Again Sides With Republicans in Political TV Ad Fight
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commission policy that gives party committees access to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates.
The court agreed to ‌let the FCC, which is chaired by Trump ally Brendan Carr, avoid a judicially imposed deadline that would have forced the agency to rule ‌on a Democratic challenge to the policy before the November 3 midterm elections. The FCC joined two Republican committees in filing a request to the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's deadline.
The court ​has a 6-3 conservative majority. Liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated they would have denied the request.
The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, modified its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March in a move seen as a boost to President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans. The president's party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November 3 midterms.
"We are pleased the Supreme Court has granted the FCC's stay request. The court's decision is right on the law and avoids the specter of upending ‌the rules for political ads right in the middle of ⁠an ongoing election," an FCC spokesperson said.
Chief Justice John Roberts had previously lifted the October 9 deadline that was given to the FCC by the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals. The 4th Circuit has accused the FCC of repeated "delay tactics" in ⁠the case, and emphasized the need for an urgent ruling in the Democratic challenge given the looming election.
The Supreme Court's latest action marks the second time in recent weeks that it has addressed the FCC's policy, as major Republican committees head toward the midterms with a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts.
In September, the court granted a request by the national Republican ​committees ​that support the party's candidates in Senate and House of Representatives races to revive the policy ​after the 4th Circuit blocked it. The justices in an ‌8-1 ruling said that the Democratic candidates must wait for the FCC to rule before filing a challenge in court.
The FCC policy at issue requires broadcasters to charge discounted rates for airing certain political advertisements within 60 days of a general election, a window that opened this year on September 4.
A group of Democratic candidates including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in April challenged the policy through in-house proceedings at the FCC. When the agency took no action, the Democrats successfully challenged the policy in the 4th Circuit, a ruling that was later halted by the Supreme Court.
The 4th Circuit on October 7 ordered the FCC to issue a prompt ruling on the ‌Democratic in-house challenge, more than five months after it was filed. In its 2-1 ruling, the ​4th Circuit said its "willingness to tolerate the FCC's delay tactics is at an end."
The Republican committees ​in their Supreme Court filing accused the 4th Circuit of having "short-circuited" the ​FCC's review process.
The Democratic candidates, for their part, accused the FCC in court papers of engaging in "blatant procedural trench warfare to stave ‌off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is ​too late to matter."
The FCC policy gained ​greater significance after the Supreme Court in June struck down federal restrictions on spending coordinated between parties and their candidates, siding with Republican challengers including Vice President JD Vance. Since the June ruling, Republican committees have blown past the former limits ahead of the midterms.
The two Republican committees have exceeded the ​former national caps by more than $48 million, according to Federal ‌Election Commission spending disclosures for July and August. Their Democratic counterparts also eclipsed the former limits, but by much less — just under $4 million.
The three ​main national Republican committees ended August with about $233 million in cash. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $130 million but also carried nearly $18 million in ​debt, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
(Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.title_orig: Archery: a living tradition at the World Nomad Games
articles.title_zh: Archery: a living tradition at the World Nomad Games
articles.content_orig:
At the beginning of September 2026, the world’s most unique multi-sport event took place in Kyrgyzstan in Central Asia. The biennial World Nomad Games attracts traditional sports athletes from nomadic and non-nomadic cultures alike – with a traditional archery competition at the heart of it.
This year, Kyrgyzstan played host for the fourth time. More than 3,000 athletes and delegates from 106 countries participated across 40 sport disciplines, spread across nine different locations. Beginning in 2014 as a gathering of 19 countries, a grand ambition has long been part of it, both as as a unifying project for the region and a projection of soft power.
The Games’ most famous and eye-catching event is kok-buru , a ferocious equestrian sport played with a goat carcass, but archery has long been a part of the nomadic cultures celebrated and was prominent in the buildup.
By far the most visible part of the competition worldwide was was the spectacular opening ceremony, held in a brand new arena in the capital Bishkek, featuring hundreds of horses ridden in formation and seen on countless social media feeds around the world.
I was part of the six-strong archery delegation from Great Britain – not a nation known for modern nomadism, but who sent just under fifty athletes across a dozen sports, with experience in each ranging from more than a decade to just a few weeks.
In traditional archery, over 250 archers from 51 countries would take part across the three days of competition. The rules required you to use the traditional bow of your country – which across Great Britain is the English longbow – and also require wooden arrows and feather fletchings with wooden nocks, although modern strings are permitted. Arrows must be shot off the hand; no shelves or rests are permitted.
The GBR team, gathered by the UK Traditional Archers' International Association, were the only athletes shooting longbows, with all other nations adopting some variety of Asiatic bow. Transporting two-metre-long one-piece wooden bows safely across the world to the shooting line was just one of the many challenges to solve.
A further rule was that you must wear the traditional national dress of your country when shooting – which is difficult, because the United Kingdom doesn't have one. With several of the team having Celtic heritage, we brewed up a concept designed to reflect and blend English, Scottish, Welsh, and Irish lineages and cultures, while still being practical to shoot in (the photo shows some of the team with the British ambassador).
The archery events were held in the extraordinary arena of the Kyrchyn Gorge, a pasture halfway up the towering mountain range that divides Kyrgyzstan from its neighbour Kazakhstan, with snow-capped ridges brooding above surrounded by swirling fog.
It's fair to say that it was a different experience from most archery competitions. The area hosted sports ranging from arm wrestling to bird hunting and even Kyrgyz sighthound racing, with weather apt to change five times in a day and precious little shelter.
The rugged nature of the location was a challenge in itself: my seat on the bus to the gorge found me sitting next to a live golden eagle, while one way in on foot required you to ford streams over stepping stones.
An enormous bazaar with a living exhibition called 'Universe Of Nomads' next door attracted tens of thousands of tourists from near and far, and the constant crowds, noise, music and woodsmoke sometimes gave the event the feel of a free festival rather than a sporting competition. You hadn't put your bow down for a minute before an enterprising local trotted up to offer you a horseback ride.
Things happened when they happened, nomad style. It was a extraordinary set of experiences, but one that required patience and endurance.
While a big part of the experience was the cultural exchange across nations, the competition was serious with some of the world's most experienced traditional archers taking part.
The three days reflected three different national traditions: Kyrgyz, Turkish, and Korean. The first day saw competition at the Kyrgyz 'Teke Buta' target shot at 40 metres, shooting nine ends of seven arrows each at an unfamiliar face featuring five scoring rings encircled by a devious mountain goat.
What made it even harder was the positional requirements; three ends were shot standing as normal, three from a reversed stance – a kind of standing Parthian shot, where our hips faced away from the target – and three ends kneeling, with knee pads provided. (I’d practised this as best I could, but it is particularly difficult with a full-length longbow.)
The Turkish 'Puta' event saw women shooting at 60 metres and men at 70 metres with a uniquely shaped hit-or-miss target, familiar to viewers of the Conquest Cup .
Finally the last day of competition saw Korean traditional competition on a massive 145 metre range at traditional Korean targets , held in almost continuous heavy rain which soaked the arrows, fletchings and archers – and made a difficult task with a longbow almost impossible. A very cold and damp set of archers left the field for the final time.
The archers participating reflected a huge variety of interests and heritage. The Australian archery delegation included Merjem Colan, who trains at the Maydaan Archery Club in Sydney, a unique club which promotes Islamic Ottoman archery heritage in the city.
Merjem and her team were some of the highest placed Western athletes in competition. “We practice Ottoman archery as more than a sport, we connect the technical skill with our history, character and community. While Australia’s traditional archery scene is spread across different organisations, that diversity gives people many ways to enter through culture, competition and craftsmanship,” she said.
“We trained through traditional Ottoman methodology, using repetition and foundational practices like kepaze and torba to develop consistency, precision and composure under pressure. But our training also develops the whole person, the internal alongside the external through discipline, patience, humility and good character,” added Merjem.
What was the most interesting part for you? “The most interesting aspect of the competition was definitely the nomadic culture. Seeing the landscape of Kyrchyn Gorge, it became clear why the nomadic tradition survives for so long in those mountains. It was beautiful to see the continuation and passing down of many of the skills from one generation to the next. Especially for me, I was amazed by the textile traditions and of course, horseback riding!”
The international traditional archery scene is governed by the World Traditional Archery Federation , who oversee an annual World Cup among much else. It maintains a living tradition that connects us not just to history, but to a dedicated global community of practitioners.
Indeed, the true value of the World Nomad Games was the vibrant celebration of shared human heritage, and we found ourselves warmly welcomed into the global nomadic tribe.
The next World Nomad Games will be held in Kazan in 2028.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Early on Wednesday, Ukraine claimed that SpaceX ( SPCX ) was restricting speed for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing invasion of the country, the Wall Street Journal reported .
"I confirm that SpaceX implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals operating in motion last night," said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, according to WSJ. "Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions."
Starlink, essentially a global broadband internet service delivered from space, is a core part of SpaceX's business . There are more than 10 million Starlink subscribers worldwide, and SpaceX is now moving to challenge legacy wireless carriers.
Ukrainian military drone crews and logistics operations regularly leverage Starlink to provide video feeds and precise targeting. WSJ reported that "Ukraine's access to SpaceX's StarShield — a Starlink subscription designed for government and military use — is provided under a contract handled by the Defense Department."
On Wednesday afternoon, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk stated that SpaceX was not involved in the latest decision to restrict those specific services.
A senior US official then told Barik Ravid of Axios that the Trump administration had nothing to do with any Starlink service constraints.
In any case, this is not the first time Ukraine has experienced Starlink throttling, though it is the first since SpaceX became a public company this summer.
In 2022, as Ukraine retook territory from Russia, Musk reportedly ordered SpaceX engineers to cut some Starlink coverage in contested areas of Ukraine. In 2023, the company acknowledged efforts to throttle Starlink usage during the war.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
"There are things that we can do to limit their ability to [leverage Starlink]," Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, said at the time. "There are things that we can do, and have done."
Musk is an ally of President Trump, who has recently ramped up criticism of Zelensky. Ukraine also bombed Russian data centers recently, disrupting bot traffic on Musk-owned X and other social media platforms.
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is not running for reelection and supports the US backing Ukraine's defense, posted on X — which Musk owns — seeking clarification on SpaceX's policy related to Starlink services.

Wisconsin-based Civic Media Inc. plans to acquire 13 radio stations and several translators in southeast Iowa and west central Illinois from the Pritchard family.
Civic Media currently owns stations in Wisconsin, Michigan, and Minnesota.
The sale, which needs FCC approval, involves stations owned by Pritchard Broadcasting Corp., Titan Broadcasting LLC and Galesburg Broadcasting Co.
Kalil & Co. served as broker for the transaction. The sale price was not disclosed.
“These stations have earned an important place in their communities through relationships they have built with listeners, local businesses and community organizations. We recognize the value of those local connections and look forward to building on that foundation as we expand our presence into these markets,” said Sage Weil, CEO and founder of Civic Media in the announcement.
Titan Broadcasting has been owned by John C. “LJ” Pritchard since 2007, according to a press release. Pritchard Broadcasting Corp. and Galesburg Broadcasting were owned and operated by John T. Pritchard until his death in August.
John C. Pritchard was quoted in the announcement, “Like my father, I believe strongly that small towns need their own media outlets to help disseminate important local information, support a vibrant business community and keep the local public informed about hyper-local matters.
“Joining the Civic Media family provides the best path forward for these stations to continue to serve the local communities today and grow and flourish long into the future,” he said.
Civic Media will acquire KGRS(FM), KBKB(AM/FM), KBUR(AM), KKMI(FM), KDMG(FM), KHDK(FM) and WQKQ(FM), in the Burlington, Iowa, market.
Also coming to Civic Media will be WLSR(FM) WGIL(AM), WKAY(FM), WAAG(FM) and WZIE(FM) in Galesburg, Ill.
Civic Media said listeners can continue to look to the stations for familiar programming.
“Across our footprint, we are committed to covering the stories most relevant to the markets we serve,” Weil said in the media release.
“We believe radio plays a crucial role in our local communities and we look forward to supporting the teams at Titan Broadcasting, Pritchard Broadcasting, and Galesburg Broadcasting Company in fulfilling that role.”
Civic Media was founded in 2022. The company calls itself a “public benefit corporation” dedicated to providing quality broadcast and digital hometown radio focusing on local, regional and state issues.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania doctors are seeing what measles can do to previously healthy, unvaccinated kids
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania doctors are seeing what measles can do to previously healthy, unvaccinated kids
articles.content_orig:
A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April.
The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman’s death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state’s health department.
In an emailed statement to The Washington Post , the coroner’s office said the primary cause of death was listed as “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.”
The previous five deaths amid the state’s measles outbreak included a newborn , a 6-week-old , an 18-year-old , a 20-year-old , and a 40-year-old . All the deceased were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
As of the latest measles update from Pennsylvania’s health department on Friday, October 9, there have been 1,136 cases in the state since the start of the year—1,124 of which are from the current outbreak. Overall, 218 people have been hospitalized. The outbreak, which now spans 41 of the state’s 67 counties, shows no signs of slowing. There had been 157 new cases reported just in the previous week.
A spokesperson for the state health department told the Post that it is “aware” of the new death and is reviewing the case. It will provide an update once the review is complete.
Measles, declared eliminated in the US in 2000, is roaring back amid misinformation and slipping vaccination rates. The nationwide measles case count for the year has hit 4,080 , the highest total since 1991. Pennsylvania’s outbreak is also the largest on record since that year . The US is widely expected to lose its measles elimination status when experts from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) meet in November to review US measles data.
Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has only included two of the six deaths so far in its reporting. There were three measles deaths reported in the US in 2025. Prior to those deaths, there had not been a measles death reported in the country since 2015.

articles.title_orig: In the cutthroat world of online dating, men use AI to put their best face forward
articles.title_zh: In the cutthroat world of online dating, men use AI to put their best face forward
articles.content_orig:
Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.
The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).
Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.
"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."
Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.
"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.
Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.
"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."
Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.
Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.
"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.
Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.
"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.
Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.
A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."
Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."
"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo slept well after cancer surgery, but recovery could take ‘longer than expected’
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo slept well after cancer surgery, but recovery could take ‘longer than expected’
articles.content_orig:
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV’s recovery from lung surgery could take “longer than expected,” the president of Peru warned Wednesday, as the leader of the Roman Catholic Church continued to mend at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital.
Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru, which was set to start Nov. 11.
“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said. “We will also be watching for any announcements from the Vatican, because we understand that his recovery will take several weeks longer than expected and, therefore, we also understand that there could be some changes to the schedule of his visit.”
Leo, who is a Chicago native , spent more than two decades working in Peru and maintains close ties with that South American country.
Fujimori’s announcement was somewhat at odds with the Vatican’s assertion on Wednesday that the pope was recovering as expected after an operation to remove part of his right lung, which confirmed a cancer diagnosis .
The medical team taking care of the 71-year-old said he had undergone routine blood tests and a chest X-ray and that, so far, the results “confirm a normal post-operative course: the values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed.”
The pope has begun walking around his hospital room and ate both breakfast and lunch on Wednesday, they said.
So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.
In the meantime, the Vatican released its first post-surgery message from the pope, which was addressed to the participants at a meeting to mark the 10th anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia,” a 2016 document on Catholic doctrine released by Pope Francis.
“As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” the message stated. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church.”
As the pontiff continues with recovery, his brother, Louis Prevost, is being treated for blood cancer, a source close to the Prevost family told NBC Chicago .
In an interview with Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty , Prevost said they’re optimistic the pope will rally.
“They caught it early enough, and he’ll be able to heal from the surgery and go on with his papal ministry,” he said.
Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.
Leo spent a calm night in the hospital after surgery to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating room for nearly three hours, it said.
The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.
Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.
The cancer diagnosis could complicate his busy schedule.
Just weeks earlier, hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor Mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence.
He was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead.
Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news.
Dr. Fernando Daniels III, a 67-year-old physician from Maryland, was among many praying for Leo’s swift recovery in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square.
“I’ve seen miracles in medicine. I’ve seen people told with terminal illnesses they wouldn’t live and they did,” he told NBC News.
“Prayers of all should heal him,” said Daniels, who was traveling as part of a group.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife, Jeanette Rubio, were praying for the pope.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.
“We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, the German Catholic news agency KNA reported.
“The pope’s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Vatican City, Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.
