articles.title_orig: Specialized ALS care linked to longer survival in real-world study
articles.title_zh: Specialized ALS care linked to longer survival in real-world study
articles.content_orig:
Benefit was strongest in people with limb-onset disease
Written by Andrea Lobo, PhD | Oct. 14, 2026
Specialized multidisciplinary care was associated with longer survival in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a study found.
The benefit was particularly notable among people with limb-onset, or spinal-onset, ALS, whose symptoms typically begin in the limbs. Median survival from symptom onset without invasive ventilation was 44 months with specialized care, compared with 25 months with general neurological care.
The researchers suggested that the survival benefit was unlikely to be explained by any single treatment. Instead, it may reflect the “cumulative effect of coordinated multidisciplinary management,” including regular follow-up, early recognition of complications, and coordinated decisions among healthcare professionals, patients, and caregivers.
The study, “ Implementation of specialised care improves survival in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ,” was published in Neurological Research and Practice .
ALS has a highly variable course. In some people, symptoms begin with weakness in the limbs, while in others they first affect speech, swallowing, or breathing.
Specialized multidisciplinary care may also affect outcomes. It can include rehabilitation, respiratory support, and nutritional management and has been associated with better outcomes in ALS. However, real-world evidence comparing general neurological care with structured, specialized care remains limited.
To investigate this, researchers at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria conducted a retrospective study comparing patients treated before and after a specialized ALS outpatient clinic was established in 2018. They examined survival, healthcare use, and treatment patterns to explore which aspects of multidisciplinary care might have contributed to differences between the groups.
The study included 242 people with ALS, of whom 106 received general neurological care and 136 received specialized multidisciplinary care. Their mean age at disease onset was about 61 years.
About two-thirds of participants had limb-onset ALS, meaning their first symptoms affected the arms or legs. About one-third had bulbar or respiratory onset, with symptoms initially affecting speech or swallowing, or breathing.
Disease stage at diagnosis did not differ significantly between the two groups. Use of treatments such as riluzole (brand names include Rilutek and Tiglutik ; generic versions are also available), feeding tubes, and invasive and noninvasive breathing support was also similar between the groups.
However, the median time from the first symptoms to ALS diagnosis was significantly longer among those receiving specialized care than among participants receiving general care (11 vs. 9 months).
Of 178 people with available data, those receiving specialized care had more hospital stays each year than patients on general care, with a median of 3.4 versus 1.2. However, the groups did not differ significantly in the number of medication groups prescribed each year or in the use of physiotherapy, occupational therapy, or speech therapy.
By the end of the study, 102 people in the general care group and 104 in the specialized care group had died. Median survival from symptom onset without invasive ventilation was significantly longer among those receiving specialized care than among patients receiving general care (40 vs. 27 months).
The difference was particularly pronounced among people with limb-onset ALS, with a median survival of 44 months with specialized care, compared with 25 months with general care. No significant survival difference was seen in the bulbar/respiratory-onset group.
Additional analyses examined survival from diagnosis rather than symptom onset. Among people with limb-onset ALS, median survival was 29 months with specialized care and 16.5 months with general care.
The survival advantage associated with specialized care was most pronounced during the first two years after diagnosis and was no longer significant thereafter. There was also no significant association between diagnostic delay and survival.
The researchers noted that the retrospective study compared patients treated during different time periods, so changes in ALS care over time or other unmeasured differences between the groups could have influenced the results.
The researchers noted that the findings “make it unlikely that the observed survival benefit is explained by the longer diagnostic delay” in the specialized care group, suggesting that specialized multidisciplinary care “exerts its greatest survival benefit early after diagnosis.”

The grenades were found to be live and active, police said.
An estate sale shopper in Austin, Texas, made an unusual call to police Tuesday after finding six World War II-era grenades in a box they had purchased at a sale.
Bomb squad officers responded to the resident's report around 4 p.m. local time Tuesday after the devices were found, according to the Austin Police Department.
The bomb squad personnel assessed the devices and determined the grenades were live and active, the Austin Police Association said in an Instagram post Tuesday.
Using X-ray imaging to help examine the devices, the personnel confirmed the grenades were live but that they did not pose an immediate threat under the circumstances, police said.
The grenades were safely seized and removed, the police association said.
"These officers bring a level of training, expertise, and steady nerves that most people never see," the police association wrote in its Instagram post. "Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work, and they do it with the professionalism this city counts on."
Patrol officers secured the area, established a perimeter and kept neighbors safe when first responding to the report, according to the police association.
It is unknown why the estate sellers were in possession of the grenades or why they were selling the box that contained them, police said.
The Austin Police Association said no one was charged with a crime in the incident and reminded the public to call 911 immediately if an old military object, such as a shell, grenade or mortar round, is found.
There is not an ongoing investigation of the incident at this time, police said.

articles.title_orig: A New World of Lung Cancer Therapy Awaits Pope Leo
articles.title_zh: A New World of Lung Cancer Therapy Awaits Pope Leo
articles.content_orig:
In a way, Pope Leo XIV may be lucky he got lung cancer now and not, say, six years ago. Treatments have changed so much, specialists say, that the old days are almost unrecognizable.
For many patients, said Karen Knudsen, the chief executive of the Parker Institute, lung cancer is no longer the dire diagnosis it was in the past.
Dr. Lecia Sequist, a thoracic oncologist at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, said, “I think a lot of people have that gut reaction about lung cancer — that it can be rapidly fatal — but that is a little bit outdated, especially if it’s caught early.”
She added, “It’s really just a whole new paradigm in lung cancer, and patients are living much longer and cure rates are higher than they were 10 to 20 years ago.”
Lung cancer is still the leading cause of cancer deaths for both men and women, killing more than 124,000 Americans each year. But the death rate today is half what it was in the 1990s, partly because fewer people smoke but also because newly developed treatments are working.
Pope Leo’s cancer, an adenocarcinoma, was discovered during a routine medical test. The pope’s doctors removed a lobe of his lung on Tuesday and are doing additional tests to determine what additional treatments, if any, are warranted.

articles.title_orig: New dinosaur species, a T. rex cousin that "would have chased us," identified from fossil found 100 years ago
articles.title_zh: New dinosaur species, a T. rex cousin that "would have chased us," identified from fossil found 100 years ago
articles.content_orig:
London — A previously unknown species of dinosaur — a "long-clawed predator the size of a tiger" and a cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex — has been identified from a fossil originally found 100 years ago, but which remained hidden away in a British museum until recently.
The species has been named Invictibellatrix amberina, and it belongs to a group of two-legged carnivores known as megaraptorans according to an article published in the Royal Society Open Science research journal.
Megaraptorans were closely related to the group of dinosaurs T. rex originated from, the tyrannosaurs. Unlike T. rex, however, scientists say Invictibellatrix did not attack prey with its mouth, but with its long arms and giant curved claws.
Researchers believe the dinosaur would have been between 10 and 13 feet long and almost 5 feet tall. Its body would have had feathers, and it would have hunted smaller dinosaurs, lizards and mammals.
The fossil that led to the discovery sat in a drawer at the Natural History Museum in London for nearly 100 years, having first been obtained by the vaunted institution in 1924.
Dr. Cassius Morrison of University College London, the lead author of the article that announced the discovery, called it a "real mystery that the fossil was overlooked for so long."
Morrison wrote that while Invictibellatrix "was not the apex predator of its time," it would have been a formidable threat to humans if they had coexisted with the species — even "more dangerous than a T. rex."
"We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight," he said. "They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small."
The fossil itself is a chunk of the back of a skull. It was one of 1,000 specimens originally discovered by Reginald Walter Tooley on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England, and it was then acquired by the Natural History Museum.
Invictibellatrix lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 120 million years ago, and is one of the smallest and earliest known members of the megaraptoran group.
To understand Invictibellatrix, researchers first took a CT scan of the fossil to create a 3D model of that part of its skull. The results were compared with the skulls of other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs, such as tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and raptors. A number of unique features led researchers to conclude they had discovered a new species.
Invictibellatrix is Latin for "unconquered female warrior" and amberina refers to the amber found in the rocks where the fossil was discovered. The researchers said by naming the dinosaur Invictibellatrix, they wanted to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in the face of such odds."

articles.title_orig: Which DP World Tour players are projected to earn 2027 PGA Tour cards?
articles.title_zh: Which DP World Tour players are projected to earn 2027 PGA Tour cards?
articles.content_orig:
Patrick Reed nearly aces No. 3, sets up birdie at Genesis Scottish Open
Ryan Fox lifted the claret jug. Ryo Hisatsune became only the second Japanese man to play in the Presidents Cup in the last 15 years. Kristoffer Reitan won a Signature Event at Quail Hollow Golf Club. Robert MacIntyre remained one of PGA Tour's top talents.
The PGA Tour is full of success stories from its strategic alliance with the DP World Tour, chief among them the pathway that provides European Tour members dual membership across both tours. That opportunity began in 2023. In just more than a month, the fourth class of Europeans will earn their Tour cards.
A refresher on how it works: After next month's DP World Tour Championship (Nov. 12-15), the top 10 finishers in the season-long Race to Dubai standings who are eligible and not otherwise exempt will earn status on the PGA Tour in 2027. That doesn’t mean specifically Nos. 1-10 in the final DP World Tour standings, since some current Tour members are inside the top 10 ( Rory McIlroy is third, for example).
The final list will likely change with four events left on the calendar, including two postseason events with elevated points available, but who are the current 10 players projected to earn Tour cards?
Reed has spent most of the season ranked No. 1 in the Race to Dubai, thanks to a first-second-first finish in a three-week span at the start of the calendar year. Reed’s lead in the points race was so large that he played the Masters, PGA Championship and U.S. Open consecutively with no starts in between, and he was still No. 1 when he returned to Europe in late June.
Now Reed’s return to the PGA Tour is imminent.
Reed hasn’t played a full season on Tour since 2021, when he won a Tour event in four consecutive seasons. Will he pick up right where he left off?
Patrick Reed's 163-yard approach sets up birdie on No. 4 at Genesis Scottish Open
The fiery Spaniard nearly won his national open last week. His runner-up finish was his third top-five finish in his last five starts and seventh overall this season. That includes back-to-back wins that Chacarra secured during the summer in France and Italy.
That form has strengthened Chacarra’s bid for a Tour card. The 26-year-old comfortably holds one of those 10 cards. A former Oklahoma State standout, the 26-year-old was teammates with multi-time PGA Tour winner Austin Eckroat in college.
Jarvis is the youngest prospective dual member at only 23 years old, and he's already a two-time winner on the DP World Tour. Jarvis was in contention (T2) for his third victory two weeks ago at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at the Old Course at St Andrews.
Like Chacarra, Jarvis won back-to-back events to vault into the top 10. He has stayed there ever since. Jarvis won his tournaments in February, claiming his first title in Kenya before winning in his native South Africa. In that spirit, Jarvis would help replenish a dwindling pipeline of top South African talent on Tour. He’s not the only one projected to do so, either.
Casey Jarvis hits tee shot to 12 feet, sets up birdie on No. 13 at 3M Open
What is it with these DP World Tour players and back-to-back wins? Schaper was the first to pull off the feat this season, winning the Alfred Dunhill Championship and the Mauritius Open way back in December.
Schaper was a decorated South African amateur. He played in the Junior World Cup and the Junior Presidents Cup (twice), won the Junior Players Championship and finished sixth at the 2020 South African Open. He was also the Sunshine Tour Rookie of the Year upon turning pro. He has steadily improved since reaching the DP World Tour, improving his rank each of the last four years. Now, he’s closing in on a Tour card.
Olesen is not here on the strength of any wins. In fact, the 27-year-old has never won on a tour recognized by the Official World Golf Ranking. He’s in position to earn his PGA Tour card because of sheer consistency.
The Dane is playing as well as anyone in Europe this fall, with seven top 20s in his last eight starts, including five top-10 finishes.
Olesen was a late bloomer. He didn’t turn pro until he was 25, the same age he won The Amateur Championship. In his debut DP World Tour season in 2025, he reached the DP World Tour Championship and shared the first-round lead at The Open Championship.
Is the former Ryder Cup player ready for a career renaissance? Sullivan was part of the losing European side at the 2016 Ryder Cup in Minnesota. It remains a career highlight for the 39-year-old, with more than 15 years of professional experience. The Englishman has four DP World Tour titles, though his last came in 2020.
Even so, Sullivan is in position to test his luck in the U.S. again.
Andy Sullivan makes birdie on No. 18 at Genesis Scottish Open
The Finnish golf product could join Sami Valimaki as the only two countrymen on Tour, a notable accomplishment for the northern European country.
As expected, Lindell was a top junior in Finland and cut his teeth in the Nordic Golf League before gradually climbing the ranks to reach the DP World Tour. After a steady rookie campaign in 2025, Lindell has two runners-up this season, which vaulted him up the standings. The 28-year-old has missed only one cut this year.
There’s still work for Lindell to do to secure a Tour card. He holds only a slim points advantage over the other three players rounding out the top 10.
Dean has walked an unlikely path in pro golf. Will it lead him to the PGA Tour? The 32-year-old Englishman ranked No. 2930 in the OWGR two years ago, working part-time as a supermarket delivery driver. His life changed on Feb. 25, 2024, when he finished tied for second at a DP World Tour event in Kenya. He repeated it later that year in France, securing an unlikely invite to The Open Championship. He played in The Open again this year, earning the lone spot available through the first-ever “Last-Chance Qualifier.”
Dean is four weeks away from an incredibly unlikely culmination of that journey.
Wiesberger is no stranger to the PGA Tour. Though he has never held full status, the 41-year-old Austrian played 10 or more Tour events in three consecutive seasons (2014-17) and made more cuts than he missed in that span, including an impressive 2017 with four top-25 finishes.
Wiesberger is also a former Ryder Cupper. He was on the losing European side at the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits. Wiesberger has nine career DP World Tour victories and is the oldest player projected to earn their Tour card via this pathway.
Bernd Wiesberger drains 19-foot birdie putt on No. 8 at Genesis Scottish Open
It was a summer to forget for Hillier as he clings to the last Tour card. The Australian was balling early in the season, with four top-six finishes in his first five starts that quickly planted him near the top of the DP World Tour standings.
Yet for as hot as Hillier was, an ice-cold midseason stretch threatened his position. Hillier missed seven of 10 cuts, which culminated at The Open at Royal Birkdale. Hillier reversed course with a T2 finish at the British Masters in late August and has now strung together four straight made cuts.
Still, with elevated points available in the final two events, Hillier is in a perilous position. He will need a strong finish to maintain his foothold on this list.

articles.title_orig: Study assesses real-world outcomes with intranasal vardenafil for ED
articles.title_zh: Study assesses real-world outcomes with intranasal vardenafil for ED
articles.content_orig:
Melissa Hadley Barrett discusses real-world outcomes and tolerability of intranasal vardenafil for men with persistent erectile dysfunction despite prior standard therapy.
In this video, Melissa Hadley Barrett discusses real-world outcomes and tolerability of intranasal vardenafil for men with persistent erectile dysfunction (ED) despite prior standard therapy. 1 Hadley Barrett is a nurse practitioner, sexologist, and founder of Restorative Health Clinic in Western Australia.
Hadley Barrett describes the rationale for evaluating intranasal vardenafil, highlighting limitations of oral phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (PDE5is), including adverse effects and the need to plan sexual activity around medication timing. In a retrospective cohort study, researchers evaluated patient-reported outcomes among men prescribed intranasal vardenafil at a specialist men's health clinic between January and December 2025. Of 505 men prescribed the medication, 147 returned outcome forms and were included in the analysis. The mean age was 65.6 years, and participants had extensive prior treatment exposure.
Overall, 68% of participants (100 of 147) reported improved Erection Hardness Score (EHS) and/or penetrative rigidity, while 53% (78 of 147) achieved penetration during intercourse. Among men with baseline EHS scores of 0 to 1, 31% (32 of 102) experienced an improvement of at least 2 points.
According to Hadley Barrett, outcomes were particularly favorable among the 45 men who switched to intranasal vardenafil because of adverse effects or inconvenience with oral PDE5is, with 93% reporting a favorable response. Treatment-emergent events were common, affecting 137 of 147 participants, but were generally mild to moderate and transient, with a median duration of 15 minutes.
These findings suggest that intranasal vardenafil may offer an alternative for selected men who remain dissatisfied with existing ED treatments. However, the retrospective design, reliance on patient-reported outcomes, and limited return of outcome forms constrain interpretation of the results. The authors emphasized that prospective controlled studies are needed to further characterize efficacy, tolerability, and the patient populations most likely to benefit.
1. Hadley Barrett M, Chung E, Whyatt D, Strange G. Real-World Outcomes and Tolerability of Intranasal Vardenafil in Treatment-Experienced Men with Persistent Erectile Dysfunction. Presented at: 27th Annual Fall Scientific Meeting of SMSNA. October 8-11, 2026. Orlando, Florida. Abstract #158

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia May Have Committed A ‘Crime’ By Claiming She’s A Lawyer, Complaint Suggests
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia May Have Committed A ‘Crime’ By Claiming She’s A Lawyer, Complaint Suggests
articles.content_orig:
A version of this story appeared in CNN’s What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .
The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news.
On that most essential qualification, the new lead White House spokeswoman, Katie Zacharia, is struggling.
She has presented herself as a lawyer but does not meet the requirements in her home state to use that title. And at least one watchdog group has asked the State Bar of California to investigate.
It’s a development made even more awkward after Republicans mercilessly attacked the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor, though he went to medical school and made his career in public health.
Zacharia has a law degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, but there’s no evidence she ever passed a bar exam. She does claim to have obtained a credential in China, but it’s not at all clear what credential she’s talking about.
Squabbles over who can call themselves a lawyer or a doctor probably seem beside the point to a large portion of the country.
This issue here is not that a law degree is required to be White House press secretary — it isn’t.
The issue is that Zacharia has presented herself repeatedly on TV, including on CNN, as a lawyer, something the independent journalist Judd Legum first documented . Trump used the term “attorney” to describe her when he announced she would be his press secretary.
A review by CNN’s K-File found at least six instances when she referred to herself as either a lawyer or a corporate lawyer in her own words and multiple other instances in which she posted or reposted to social media using the term attorney or “legal strategist.”
Washington, DC, is filled to the brim with people who have law degrees but do not practice law. And it does not appear that Zacharia inappropriately tried to represent anyone in a court.
But all of this does suggest the vetting operation at the White House is, to be charitable, not very thorough.
When reporters asked Trump at the White House where Zacharia passed the bar, she chimed in from behind him that she was when she moved to China. Even Trump did a double take.
Zacharia later told Politico she had “practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
It’s not clear — and the White House has not clarified — what certification Zacharia obtained in China, but it’s not the Chinese version of the bar exam. Only citizens can become licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice .
Questions about Zacharia’s CV are also an awkward development since Republicans in Michigan have attacked the Democrat running for Senate there, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor despite having gone to medical school.
At a debate this month, the Republican in the Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers, went so far as to say El-Sayed was a “con man.”
As CNN has reported , El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine.
El-Sayed has held public health positions in the Detroit area. His top policy issue is extending health insurance to all Americans.
Democratic boosters of El-Sayed have continued to call him a doctor.
“Abdul’s a doctor, and he’s taken on special interests to fight for good jobs, better healthcare, and lower costs,” former President Barack Obama said in an ad he cut for the Michigander.
In addition to saying on TV that she is a lawyer, Zacharia cites some legal-sounding work on her LinkedIn page; for example, she lists herself as “general counsel” for the activist group Fix California. In the nonprofit group’s tax filing for 2024, Zacharia’s name appears as having been a fundraiser.
She also lists herself as having worked as an “associate” in the international practice group at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011.
The White House press corps, obviously, has followed up on this mystery.
“Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law,” according to a White House official.
CNN’s White House team has found no evidence that Zacharia has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating from Pepperdine.
Here’s what California’s bar association told them:
California law lays out what’s required to be a lawyer.
There are requirements for college and law school, or their equivalents; for “good moral character”; passing an ethics exam; and passing the bar exam in California.
Zacharia, as a result, should not be considered a lawyer in California, the state where she has lived and worked.
A separate section of California law makes it a misdemeanor to pretend to be a lawyer.
Does presenting oneself as a lawyer on TV violate that piece of code?
The group Campaign for Accountability, which describes itself as a nonpartisan government watchdog, on Wednesday announced it had asked the State Bar of California to investigate.
Many other questions remain. What is the credential Zacharia obtained in China, if any? Did she try to take a bar exam and fail, or simply not take it? Why did no one at the White House, especially after questions arose about El-Sayed’s status as a doctor, think to follow up on this earlier?
None of that really matters to anyone who is more concerned with how the White House is handling the war Trump launched on Iran or the related inflation that continues to hit Americans in the wallet. Questions about whether Zacharia can call herself a lawyer, or not, mostly distract from those other, larger issues.
Ultimately, Trump is the person who speaks for his administration in the long, often rambling appearances he frequently makes in the Oval Office.
But those appearances may become less enjoyable for him in the future, especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress and, as expected, launch a series of investigations into his administration, the money his family has made during his presidency, and much more.
He will, at that point, need a press secretary he can trust.
CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: ‘Longest eight seconds in the world’
articles.title_zh: ‘Longest eight seconds in the world’
articles.content_orig:
LAS VEGAS – The broncs and bulls were buckin’ Tuesday as Native cowboys and cowgirls showed why they are among the best rodeo athletes in the world on Day One of the Indian National Finals Rodeo.
Celebrating its 50th anniversary, the event draws athletes from all around Indian Country to Las Vegas to compete for gold buckles and world championships. They come from north of the Medicine Line to the southwest, Oregon to Florida and everywhere in between.
Some are veterans, attending Indian Country’s biggest rodeo year after year. Others, like Hannah Joy Fleury, made the trek for the first time.
Fleury, Tlingit and Haida, flew in from Alaska to the South Point Equestrian Center in Las Vegas for her first INFR experience. She said it was fun and exciting, citing bull riding as her favorite event of both the afternoon and evening performances.
“Eight seconds is the longest eight seconds in the world, it’s fun,” Fleury told ICT . “I’m like, ‘What do you mean they gotta stay on eight seconds?’”
When asked what she thought goes through a bull rider’s mind before the chute opens, she figured it was pretty simple.
On the other end of that spectrum, Terry Tatsey, Blackfeet, has been in attendance since the INFR moved to Las Vegas 18 years ago. His first Indian finals was back in 1986 when it was hosted at the Tingley Coliseum in Albuquerque, New Mexico. He competes in the senior championship division these days.
The biggest change over the years, he said, has not only been the number of spectators who take in the rodeo but also the level of competition.
“A lot of the contestants that are in the PRCA [Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association] right now have used this venue as a way to establish themselves in their career, and then they move on to the professional and even compete at the National Finals Rodeo,” Tatsey said.
While he enjoys watching all aspects of rodeo, he enjoys the timed events – as that is what he competes in – as well as the team events because of the horsemanship involved.
“It goes back to a lot of our old culture,” Tatsey told ICT . “Our people trained horses, buffalo running horses or horses for moving camp, so that relationship and communication between horse and rider is always good to watch.”
Norma Wauneka, Navajo, is a former competitor turned spectator. Her daughter, Justine Begay is a former INFR World Champion who also took first place in Round 1 of the Ladies Breakaway event.
Watching her daughter rope is the highlight of Norma’s INFR week and she also enjoys seeing old friends she’s made on the rodeo circuit over the years.
“With rodeo, you meet people all over the country, and you have friends, like I said, from Florida to Canada,” Wauneka said. “If I didn’t do rodeo, I wouldn’t have met those friends and lifetime friends, and they’re great. It’s like family. Rodeo’s family. When you meet somebody, you know, they take care of you.”

articles.title_orig: Cardinal Tagle reads Pope Leo's homily to bishops: 'The world has no future without strong families'
articles.title_zh: Cardinal Tagle reads Pope Leo's homily to bishops: 'The world has no future without strong families'
articles.content_orig:
Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, pro-prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization, celebrates a Mass in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican Oct. 14, 2026, on the final day of a meeting in which the presidents of bishops' conferences marked the 10th anniversary of "Amoris Laetitia" ("The Joy of Love"). The Mass also included special prayers for the health of Pope Leo XIV following his lung surgery the previous day and diagnosis of cancer. (OSV News/Reuters/Stoyan Nenov)
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the newly elected dean of the College of Cardinals, presided over the closing Mass for the Vatican meeting of bishops on marriage and family on Oct. 14, reading aloud a homily that had been prepared by Pope Leo XIV prior to his lung cancer surgery, saying, "The world has no future without strong families."
Leo had been scheduled to preside over the closing Mass in St. Peter's Square himself before he shocked the world on Sunday with the announcement that he would be having surgery. As a result, the morning Mass took place without the presence of the pope, just hours after the Vatican announced that late Oct. 13 that the surgery had confirmed a diagnosis of lung cancer for the 71-year-old pope.
Participants in the Oct. 7-14 gathering of the world’s bishops’ conference presidents and the heads of Eastern Catholic churches marking the 10th anniversary of Pope Francis' document on the family, Amoris Laetitia , prayed for Leo's recovery in the Prayer of the Faithful during the Mass and listened to the words that the pope had prepared for them.
"The world has no future without strong families open to the gift of children and attentive to their education and growth," Leo wrote in his homily, which emphasized the important role of families in educating and forming the young in the virtues.
The pope highlighted, quoting Amoris in part, that "the importance of the virtues, among which a special place is given to chastity, which is 'invaluable for the genuine growth of love between persons,'" in preparing young people for true love in marriage.
"Marriage preparation programs conscientiously developed for this purpose in parishes and pastoral areas are commendable. Yet such courses alone are insufficient, for they must be preceded and supported by an education in love that accompanies a person’s growth from childhood," he wrote.
Leo highlighted Francis' post-synodal apostolic exhortation that followed the Synod on the Family, saying that "marriage preparation begins at birth."
"In this way, love lived within the family — with its moments of struggle, mistakes and failures, yet also with the marvel of its unpredictable, everyday life — becomes the first school of human affection, the first precious and irreplaceable apprenticeship in the 'joy of love,'" Leo said.
Leo said that "the values of openness to life and respect for life, from conception to natural death, are also rooted in this charity, which is fundamental to our existence and to our life together as human beings."
"The family is the foremost guardian of these values, a beacon for the good of humanity," he added.
As Tagle read aloud the pope's prepared homily, the cardinal noted the presence of Patriarch Paul III Nona, the patriarch of Baghdad of the Chaldeans, whom Leo granted ecclesiastical communion in April.
"I myself have the honor of presiding over this celebration by special mandate of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV, in order to manifest publicly the ecclesiastical communion he has granted to His Beatitude Paul III Nona, Patriarch of Baghdad of the Chaldeans, who is participating in this Eucharist," the cardinal said.
"Your Beatitude, your presence helps us better understand our identity as the Church, which is a communion in Christ the Lord of the Churches of various rites and traditions, in a unity that is expressed tangibly with the Successor of Peter," he added.
The Vatican did not provide an update on Leo's clinical condition in the morning following the announcement of his cancer diagnosis, other than that the pope's first night in the hospital passed calmly.
Following the closing Mass, the bishops, families and experts taking part in the Amoris Laetitia meeting are scheduled to meet again in the late afternoon for the presentation of the meeting's synthesis report at the closing session of the weeklong event.
Due to the personal request of Leo prior to his surgery, the meeting's final synthesis report will no longer be made public on Oct. 14. Jesuit Fr. Giacomo Costa, a consultant to the General Secretariat of the Synod, said that the pope requested to postpone the meeting's final report, noting that Leo "wanted to listen to it and be able to offer his own word on it himself."

articles.title_zh: HomeView will support video apps like YouTube, Netflix—if they say yes
articles.content_orig:
Apple unveiled its new HomeView product yesterday ( pre-order here ), but the device’s support for third-party apps was initially unclear. A newly published Apple document , however, offers good news about HomeView supporting third-party video apps like YouTube and Netflix.
Yesterday when Apple announced the HomeView, it said surprisingly little about third-party apps.
HomeView doesn’t have an App Store, so you won’t be able to download third-party apps like on iPhone. However, support for some audio and video apps was vaguely confirmed by Apple .
Today we’ve learned new details, including as relates to which video apps will be compatible. In a newly updated CarPlay Developer Guide , Apple says:
CarPlay audio and video apps also work on Apple HomeView without requiring you to make any modifications to your app. […]
Apps with CarPlay audio app (CarPlay framework) or CarPlay video app entitlements appear on Apple HomeView.
Video apps for CarPlay were newly introduced this year in iOS 27. But they require automakers to explicitly support CarPlay’s video feature—which most don’t. As a result, developers have had little reason to make their video apps compatible with CarPlay.
But HomeView will change that in a big way.
Now major players like YouTube, Netflix, and Disney+ will be able to make their apps appear on HomeView simply by adding CarPlay support.
I think it’s imperative that video apps are on Homeview. It’s a pretty bare device without that support. I’m wondering why they never showed this with the marketing video, and it seems they’re maybe having issues getting the support. It felt strange there was no part of the video showing someone watching Disney or Netflix. I suspect Spotify will throw their usual wobbly as well, because it looked like only Apple Music and Podcasts, unless I’ve missed something.
HomeView now provides these developers a great reason to invest in making CarPlay-compatible apps. And that investment will benefit not only HomeView owners, but CarPlay users too.
I might be overly optimistic, but I suspect major video apps will be eager to support Apple’s new HomeView product as soon as possible. Perhaps we’ll even see several of them available before the November 13 launch.
You can pre-order HomeView starting at $289 for select models.
Do you expect third-party video apps to add HomeView support? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Why Trump is likely to join Saudi war against Houthis
articles.title_zh: Why Trump is likely to join Saudi war against Houthis
articles.content_orig:
The admin might have been toying with MBS, but it won't be able to resist certain pressures for long, say QI experts
For myriad obvious reasons, President Donald Trump has so far resisted calls from Saudi Arabia to assist in its fight with the Houthis, even as the militant group has been striking — literally — at the heart of the Kingdom's oil and tourism industries all week.
First, the U.S. can hardly afford another front in its current Middle East war. We know Pentagon munitions stockpiles are depleted , and our main asset in the region, the U.S. Navy, is stretched thin trying to manage its blockade against Iran and helping to shuttle non-sanctioned shipping through the Strait of Hormuz (which is not going as well as the White House was boasting a week ago).
Second, politically, Trump cannot afford to launch another war ahead of the midterms, especially if it is not guaranteed to be successful. His first escalation against the Houthis in 2025 failed, and he was forced to call a ceasefire . The Yemeni resistance group, also known as Ansar Allah, has only gotten stronger since.
But the pressure is on, and Annelle Sheline, research fellow at the Quincy Institute's Middle East program, says it is likely that Trump will be forced to get involved sooner than later.
"P art of why we've seen the Trump administration not give in to Mohammed bin Salman's request to engage directly in attacking Ansar Allah inside Yemen is because the Saudis kicked the Emiratis out of Yemen last January," Sheline told me this morning, referring to remnants of the two nation's joint involvement in the first Yemeni Civil War.  "T he U.S. is very closely aligned with the UAE, which is obviously very closely aligned with Israel , and so there's a sense from the administration that the Saudis made their bed and now they need to lie in it. But that does imply that after Trump feels that the Saudis have been made to suffer, then he will get involved more directly."
Perhaps even more urgently, MBS may put on the table all of its investments in the U.S. that Trump had only been touting a year ago when he did his much ballyhooed tour of the Middle East. At the time he said he got pledges for $1 trillion from the region, including $600 billion from Saudi Arabia. A $ 142 billion arms deal was also announced at the time.
"Just given how we know things work in Washington, there are obviously many pressures from the U.S. defense industry, from the the fact that Mohammed bin Salman has personally enriched Trump and his family, including Jared Kushner's various expensive endeavors," Sheline said, noting the president's son-in-law's close investment ties with the Kingdom, which are now a focus of a congressional investigation .
"So I don't think it will be too long before Mohammed bin Salman says to Donald Trump, 'Look, I'm not going to ask again if you don't assist us. We're going to have to reconsider investments in the United States. We're going to have to reconsider investments in in your family, in the Trump brand,' and I imagine that may hit Trump a little closer to home."
The Quincy Institute's Trita Parsi said he agrees the U.S. lurch in defense of Saudi Arabia is likely, but thinks Trump may wait for the midterms. "I think Trump's preference is for it to happen afterwards. But it may not be under his control if he sees further escalation by Iran or the Houthis," he told me.
It is definitely on the president's mind. In response to a direct question of involvement on Sunday he said, " We're gonna look at it … We'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
On Tuesday he said the Houthis were "behaving very badly" and blamed the group for attacking Saudi Arabia to purposely spike oil prices before the midterms . Meanwhile, CBS News speculated that the death of an American in the Houthi attack on Riyadh's biggest airport on Saturday, "may increase pressure on Mr. Trump to retaliate."

articles.title_orig: Seeking Gospel hope in a world increasingly shaped by AI
articles.title_zh: Seeking Gospel hope in a world increasingly shaped by AI
articles.content_orig:
Author: Br. Steven Patti, OFM
Date Published: October 14, 2026
How can we stay rooted in the dignity of the human person amid rapidly advancing technology? Br. Steven Patti, OFM, recently considered that question with parishioners at St. Camillus Church in Silver Spring, Maryland, during a series of discussions on Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. In this reflection, Br. Steven shares what they discerned about AI, human dignity and the hope found in the Gospel.
Br. Jorge Hernandez, OFM, pastor of St. Camillus Church, asked me if I would give a reflection on Pope Leo’s recent encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas. And so, for three successive Saturdays in September, for two hours each session, a group of us met in the Francis Room to discuss the encyclical, with chairs set up in a circle around the room.
Most had heard about the encyclical, but few, if any, had read it. They were curious and interested in learning more. We looked at several questions: What is an encyclical? What is Leo doing in this encyclical? What did we find in it over our three sessions?
Magnifica Humanitas is lengthy, and much of it is rooted in the Bible and in Catholic Social Teaching. Leo XIV refers to his predecessor in name, Leo XIII, and to Leo’s Rerum Novarum, which addressed the rising industrialization of the late 19th century. We talked about how it was no accident that our modern Leo chose his papal name: Both popes show a deep concern for the centrality of the human person amid rising industrialization and technology, 135 years apart.
Br. Steven Patti, OFM, said participants in a discussion about Magnifica Humanitas expressed concern about the fate of humans, given the rapid rise of artificial intelligence. (Photo courtesy of Br. Steven)
This resonated with people. The group expressed fears: What is happening to our world around us? Where is, and what is the fate of, “the person,” the human person, amid an emerging world of AI? What and whom can I trust amid rising disinformation, surveillance and data collection, and AI as a social companion? What does it mean when AI gives answers without any authentic sense or knowledge of mercy and compassion? What does AI mean for the future of warfare?
‘Humanity at risk’ was a common topic of conversation among the group, along with a sense that the human person is increasingly becoming a cog in a machine. There was also a sense of gratitude for the pope’s words, for his speaking publicly and prophetically about an issue that seems to develop in new ways daily.
In the discussions Br. Steven Patti, OFM, led, he mentioned that Pope Leo XIV reminds us who we are called to be during a social shift that can at times feel baffling and confusing. (Photo courtesy of Br. Steven)
But the news was not all grim. Even amid an ever-changing technological landscape, Magnifica Humanitas points to the Gospel, to who we are as disciples of Christ in our modern world. Leo reminds us who we are called to be amid this often bewildering and disorienting social change.
He writes beautifully and with hope: “Even in the darkest nights, the Lord raises up men and women who refuse to give up, who persevere in doing good, who protect the vulnerable and open pathways to reconciliation” (MH 211). He adds, “Do not think that the problems are too big, and that we are too small” (MH 212).
And so, what did we find after three Saturday morning sessions?
It felt like modern Church: a naming of the signs of the times, shared voices around the circle, and a shared sense that the Gospel and our entire Christian tradition root us in the centrality and dignity of the human person and in how we are called to follow in the footsteps of Jesus.
As Pope Leo ends his encyclical: “With the same faith as Mary, let us become weavers of hope in our world, sharing who we are and what we have, so that the presence of Jesus may grow among us and his kingdom take shape” (MH 245).

articles.title_orig: Real-World Data Expand Evidence for Mogamulizumab in CTCL
articles.title_zh: Real-World Data Expand Evidence for Mogamulizumab in CTCL
articles.content_orig:
Real-world German MINT data show mogamulizumab delivers durable responses, ~20-month PFS, manageable safety, and improved quality of life in MF and Sézary syndrome.
Mogamulizumab (Poteligeo) was associated with durable real-world treatment outcomes in patients with mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS), according to final results from the German MINT study. 1
In this real-world analysis, treatment with mogamulizumab was associated with an overall response rate of 62.4% and a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 20.2 months. Among 109 patients, the median time to next treatment was 14.9 months, providing additional data on treatment duration in routine clinical practice.
“For patients living with [MF] and [SS], understanding how treatments perform outside the controlled setting of clinical trials is critically important,” Chalif Assad, MD, of Helios Klinikum Krefeld, Health and Medical University Düsseldorf-Krefeld in Germany, stated in a news release. “The final MINT results demonstrate meaningful clinical outcomes across a broad patient population treated in routine practice and highlight the value of collaborative real-world research in helping clinicians make informed treatment decisions.”
MINT (Mogamulizumab in a Non-interventional Study to Evaluate the Safety and Outcome in Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome Treatment) was a multicenter, noninterventional study conducted at 18 centers across Germany. The analysis included 56 patients with MF and 53 with SS, with a median follow-up of 25.2 months. Most patients (83.5%) had advanced disease, defined as stage IIB or higher, at treatment initiation.
Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 38.5% of patients, with drug eruption and lymphopenia among the most commonly reported events. Serious TRAEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 22.0% of patients. The overall safety profile was described as consistent with findings from the phase 3 MAVORIC trial (NCT01728805), which supported mogamulizumab’s FDA approval in CTCL in August 2018. 2
Quality of life improved during treatment, with median Skindex-29 scores decreasing from 49.1 at baseline (n = 21) to 30.2 at month 12 (n = 7), representing a 38.5% improvement. However, the small number of patients with available month 12 assessments limits interpretation of this finding.
The MINT findings complement results from MAVORIC, which compared mogamulizumab with vorinostat (Zolinza) in 372 patients with previously treated MF or SS. In MAVORIC, median PFS was 7.7 months with mogamulizumab vs 3.1 months with vorinostat (HR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.41-0.69; P <.0001). 3
Together, the studies contribute to the evidence base for mogamulizumab in MF and SS, with MINT extending observations to a real-world population that included a high proportion of patients with advanced disease. However, the observational design and limited sample sizes in certain subgroups underscore the need for caution when interpreting these findings.

The Motor Mart Garage, a century-old Art Deco structure on the border of Bay Village and Back Bay that was once the world’s largest parking garage, has sold at a massive discount.
Boston real estate development firm Related Beal and Freeport Equity, a real estate investor based in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., closed on the long-rumored acquisition this week. The partnership bought the Motor Mart property for $89 million, a 45 percent discount from the garage’s prior sale price, according to a source with direct knowledge of the deal who spoke on condition of anonymity. As of midday Wednesday, the deal had not yet been recorded in Suffolk County property records.
“Motor Mart sits at the heart of a neighborhood we have been investing in for many years and holds great possibility for future residential and commercial development,” said Kimberly Sherman Stamler, president of Related Beal, in a statement.
The 1,037-space garage is the latest in a long line of properties in Boston and beyond that have sold for less than their prior purchase price, though few sales have seen as dramatic a discount as the Motor Mart. This summer, Oxford Properties Group bought a Seaport District office that’s 99 percent leased for $435 million, a 10 percent discount from its previous sale. Meanwhile, the 32-story, 1.1 million-square-foot tower at 100 Summer St. is set to be sold at foreclosure auction next week.
Some $1.26 trillion of commercial real estate mortgages are expected to come due next year, up from $950 billion in 2024, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . That will create big opportunities for real estate investors hunting for bargains — but also could see a lot of firms losing a lot of money.
“That is going to present a great deal of opportunity. It’s also going to present some pain,” said Ian Brandon, the chief commercial banking officer for Cambridge Savings Bank, at a Wednesday event hosted by real estate news and events company Bisnow.
Los Angeles-based CIM Group spent $162.5 million a decade ago to acquire the Motor Mart Garage, which spans 1.2 acres.
CIM later clinched city approval to build a 20-story condominium tower that would rise 310 feet from within the existing building. The approved project was set to include 231 condos, a ninth-floor roof deck, and possibly a grocery store. The project never got off the ground.
At the time of its approval — October 2019, just before the world-upending COVID-19 pandemic — CIM estimated the tower would cost $525 million to build. Today, that would be at least $775 million, according to a Globe analysis of federal construction pricing data .
A CIM representative did not immediately respond Wednesday to a request for comment. Stamler did not share further information about Related Beal’s plans for the property.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported the percentage change between the Motor Mart’s last sale and its 2016 sale price. It is 45 percent. The Globe regrets the error.

articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, according to new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was facing mounting scrutiny over allegations she asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration and behaved inappropriately while in Athens.
Trump said on Tuesday that she had done a good job, but will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.
Guilfoyle acknowledged that her time as ambassador was "coming to an end", though vowed to defend herself and called the claims against her "false".
The ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime", she added in her comments on X.
Guilfoyle was "asked to resign", said Zacharia during her first - and unusually short - White House media briefing. She did not provide further details.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," Zacharia said.
Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
Around the same time, news broke that she had broken up with Donald Trump Jr, to whom she was engaged.
In her lengthy post on X on Tuesday, Guilfoyle thanked the elder Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.
"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding that she would "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".
Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on behalf of Deters before she became ambassador.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.
Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".
Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.
Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with Trump Jr. They became engaged in 2018 and broke up in late 2024.
Trump said on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member.
The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign.
"She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.
The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.
Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.
For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration saw as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family, and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.
She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

articles.title_orig: Epic’s new games launcher is ‘vibe coded’
articles.title_zh: Epic’s new games launcher is ‘vibe coded’
articles.content_orig:
Epic is making a big push into AI-assisted development, and that approach includes its work on the new, faster launcher.﻿
Epic is making a big push into AI-assisted development, and that approach includes its work on the new, faster launcher.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Epic Games is announcing a big refresh of its PC games launcher today in preview, saying that the new version is “way faster” and now supports Linux. But the company, which has been publicly making a big push into AI-assisted development, also notes that the refresh was “vibe coded.”
“Programming is hard,” Epic says in a blog post . “So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.”
On Monday, CEO Tim Sweeney announced that the company has a “huge pivot underway,” where it will be “moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration.” Sweeney said the aim “isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.” Bloomberg also reported this week that an Epic director on an unannounced Disney title told staffers that there would be “No more hand-written code.”
“We used AI as a tool for this,” Martin Keely, Epic’s VP and GM of the Epic Games Store and Epic Online Services, tells The Verge in a briefing about the launcher. “It’s part of our migration as a company to use AI in new and different ways.” Keely says that AI has been “super helpful” for testing and for “replicating the core functionality from the existing launcher,” and he also notes that it’s also allowing Epic to offer the new launcher on Linux.
Epic has been working on the launcher for “most of this year,” Keely says, and while AI has helped Epic “accelerate our development,” the team working on the new launcher hasn’t adopted the “no more hand-written code” model reported on by Bloomberg . “We definitely had agents write and review all of the code,” Keeley says. “We used it to replicate the core functionality.” But the development team “managed that process” and “supervised the entirety of what we did.”
Still, while the launcher team’s approach predates what Sweeney announced this week, “it’s on the same train,” Keely says. “The launcher is something that is demonstrative of the speed and efficiency both from the development process and the actual output that we think gives us confidence that the direction that we’re headed in is a positive one for our company and for gaming development overall.”
The new Epic Games Launcher preview will be available on Windows, Mac, and Linux beginning today, and the old version will remain available. (Alongside the Linux version of the launcher, Epic is also announcing that it plans to bring Fortnite to Linux through the app.) Epic doesn’t have a specific timeline for when everyone will have to move over to the new version, Keely says, but the company will do the full launch when the update feels “stable” and has parity in “all places that we need” with the current launcher.
In March, Epic laid off more than 1,000 staffers. “Since it’s a thing now, I should note that the layoffs aren’t related to AI,” Sweeney said in a memo to staff at the time . “To the extent it improves productivity, we want to have as many awesome developers developing great content and tech as we can.”

articles.title_orig: Bloomfield Students Get an Inside Look at the World of Game Development
articles.title_zh: Bloomfield Students Get an Inside Look at the World of Game Development
articles.content_orig:
From playtesting games to connecting with the people who create them, Bloomfield students get a glimpse of the opportunities available in the world of game development.
For Bloomfield College of Montclair State University students passionate about video games, a recent trip to the 2026 Game Devs of Color Expo NYC Watch Party offered a chance to explore the industry beyond the classroom. Open to students across all Creative Arts and Technology (CAT) majors, the field trip gave attendees the opportunity to experience the world of game development firsthand.
The Game Devs of Color Expo is a virtual conference that brings together game creators to showcase their work, share their experiences and celebrate the creativity and diversity of the gaming community. For the first time, the NYC Watch Party gave Bloomfield students the opportunity to experience the online event in person alongside local developers, fellow students and gaming enthusiasts.
Throughout the event, students explored game stations featuring independent titles, tried out games created by developers and watched presentations highlighting different perspectives and experiences in the industry. The Watch Party also provided opportunities to speak with attendees about their work and learn more about the creative process behind developing games.
“So much of game design is about community, and meeting developers means our students can start building those connections on their own terms." — GJ Lee, associate professor of Creative Arts and Technology
The virtual conference gave students a chance to learn more about the gaming industry from the people working in it. Through presentations and discussions, they heard different perspectives on game development, from the creative decisions behind a game to the experiences of those building careers in the field.
For Game Programming major Tim Fuentes, the Expo offered a closer look at the industry he hopes to one day be part of.
“I’ve always been into video games since I was very young, and I want to become a game programmer,” Fuentes says. “I thought this field trip would be a good opportunity to meet professional game programmers and see how the space works.”
One of the highlights of the conference was seeing the variety of ideas being brought to life by independent creators. Games can take many different forms, and the presentations offered a look at how developers use storytelling, technology and their own experiences to create something unique.
GJ Lee , associate professor in Bloomfield's Creative Arts and Technology program, accompanied the students to the Watch Party, also sees value in introducing students to the community surrounding game development.
“So much of game design is about community, and meeting developers means our students can start building those connections on their own terms,” says Lee.
By bringing the virtual conference and in-person Watch Party together, the event gave Bloomfield students a chance to learn about the industry while experiencing the community that makes it all possible.
Bloomfield Faculty in the Gaming Industry
Bloomfield's involvement in the Game Devs of Color Expo goes beyond the student field trip. Professor G.J. Lee helped open the virtual conference alongside its directors, while fellow faculty member Hatim Benhsain had his game, coalescent || tidal rapture , featured at the event.
Benhsain is developing the 3D swimming adventure game through his studio, Games for my Computer. The game follows a society of merpeople undergoing evolution and explores themes of queer relationships and connection.
“It was a huge honor to have our game featured,” Benhsain says. “We are so excited to share coalescent with the whole wide world, and this helped us get closer to that goal.”
Having faculty members involved in events like the Expo gives students another way to see how the work happening in their classrooms connects to the gaming industry. For aspiring developers, it's a chance to learn from professors who are also contributing their own creative work to the field.
With opportunities to learn from industry professionals, discover independent projects and see their own professors' work represented at the conference, students left with a broader picture of the possibilities ahead of them in game development.

articles.title_orig: How technology is changing the detection of breast cancer
articles.title_zh: How technology is changing the detection of breast cancer
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Rachel Brem decided at age 12 that she wanted to cure cancer after her mom was diagnosed with breast cancer. It was early detection that led to her mother living way past her prognosis of six months. Now, Brem is working to improve breast cancer screening for all women.
Brem is a board-certified diagnostic radiologist and director of Breast Imaging and Intervention at George Washington University. She created the Brem Foundation to help prevent breast cancer from taking more lives.
On this week's episode of "Healthful," she discussed the innovation that makes her hopeful.
"AI is going to change everything in medicine, and certainly breast cancer detection," Brem said.
In addition to her work with George Washington University's Breast Imaging and Intervention unit, Brem collaborates with ScreenPoint Medical to develop Transpara, an AI breast cancer screening software.
Already there is significant scientific research showing mammograms paired with AI evaluations "can find cancer up to five years earlier," she said, by detecting warning signs in women that might be missed with just mammograms alone. The software can also predict future risk of breast cancer even when none is detected in a mammogram.
"Imagine what the impact of that is going to be on survival therapy," Brem said.
If women begin getting screened at age 35 with AI-enhanced readings, she noted the software will constantly teach itself how to improve in detecting breast cancer with each analysis. That's younger than the starting age recommended by several major medical organizations.
At George Washington University, Brem said, "we've been using AI for over four years in every mammogram," adding that using the software does not cost extra.
The FDA has cleared some AI technology to predict risk of or detect breast cancer.
However, nationwide, just 20% of practices use AI with their mammogram procedures. Often, the AI readings cost extra, which may make the option inaccessible for some.
"There is nothing you can do to absolutely prevent breast cancer," Brem acknowledged.
But she said, "One of the things AI can do is really equalize the inequalities," referring to the racial disparities that affect diagnosis and treatment for many women.
"Black women die at a 40% higher rate [from breast cancer] than White women," Brem noted, and women with fewer resources have less access to mammograms.
Brem wants to change this with her foundation , which for the past 20 years has championed early detection  through innovative screening, increased education and awareness, and equitable access.
"I look forward to the more wide-reaching implementation of AI to help not only find more cancers, but with healthcare," she said.
Brem is helping to develop a breath test that could detect breast cancer. Diseased tissues give off a chemical compound that becomes gas and, scientists believe, could be used as a noninvasive way to assess who needs further screening.
These tests are still in the experimental and clinical trial phases. They are not cleared by the FDA for screening.
"It's not available yet, but I'm really excited about having no pain, no compression, and no injection way of diagnosing if you're accurately diagnosed," Brem said.
And there's hope it could someday help beyond breast cancer. "The next step on our roadmap is not just breast cancer but a women's health panel where you could do one breath and get all these tests done," Brem said.
The guidelines from the American College of Physicians stated in 2026 that women over the age of 50 should get a mammogram every other year. The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends that women should start screening every other year at the age of 40.
To Brem, "This is a travesty."
"Women will die if they listen to that."
From her research, women should get checked for breast cancer annually starting at the age of 40. For those with a history of breast cancer in their family, they should start at 35.
This is all easier said than done. Women often cite anxiety as a reason they delay or skip getting screened. The thought of receiving a positive test result understandably makes women nervous, but as Brem notes, "We don't get rid of the disease by not knowing we have it."
Early detection of breast cancer leads to significantly better outcomes compared to cases where breast cancer is found in its later stages.
"Ninety-nine percent of women with early breast cancer survive and thrive," Brem said, but this outcome can only be possible if women screen for it early and regularly.
In addition to the recommended mammograms, Brem also believes "you absolutely, unequivocally definitely need more exams" if you have dense breasts . Half of women have dense breasts, and mammograms might not be able to pick up potentially deadly tumors hiding behind the tissue. Ultrasounds, MRIs or contrast-enhanced mammograms are necessary for those with dense breasts to get a complete view of their risks.
Supplemental screening isn't always standard with some doctors. Brem advised that it is "really important" for women to insist that their doctors order these extra exams. The mammograms are not enough.
Brem is adamant in her belief that women can be proactive now to better their health and improve their breast cancer outcomes. If you have dense breasts, demand additional screening.
For those under 40 who think they have time until they need to start screening for breast cancer, think again.
"You're not too young to have breast cancer," Brem warns.
Having the conversation now about your plan for breast cancer screenings and seeking out additional exams is essential in early detection and better prognosis. "If you find it early, even if you're young, it's curable," Brem said.
Rates of cancer are rising in younger women and awareness is the first step to being proactive about your health. Her foundation provides resources to educate women.
But what do you do with this information? Brem urges you to advocate for yourself at the doctor's office.
"We tell women to be badass," she said. "You need to advocate for yourself. It is a fundamental principle. It's your right. It's what you deserve, and it's not a maybe."

articles.title_orig: As Ebola spreads in eastern Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
articles.title_zh: As Ebola spreads in eastern Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
articles.content_orig:
The latest numbers from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) show the Ebola outbreak now stands at 9,066 cases 4,381 deaths. This is the second largest Ebola outbreak in history, following the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
The West Africa outbreak was caused by the more common Zaire strain of the virus. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, which has no approved treatments or vaccines. The outbreak’s current case-fatality rate is 48.2%.
Today CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, announced preparations are under way for a phase 2/3 trial called Tumaini, which will evaluate the safety, immunogenicity and efficacy of vaccine candidates against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), including Ervebo, the Zaire-targeting vaccine.
“Tumaini is designed as an adaptive platform trial, subject to ethical and regulatory approval,” CEPI said . “This allows several vaccine candidates to be evaluated in parallel within a single trial framework, which saves valuable time during an outbreak.” In addition to Ervebo, the trial will include at least two Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates.
Currently the Bravo study, a research project coordinated by Doctors Without Borders (Medecins sans Frontieres) is evaluating the effectiveness of the Ervebo vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain in North Kivu and Ituri province. Teams have vaccinated 857 frontline workers.
Late last week the US Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory confirmed the detection of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) on two Yakima County dairy farms in Washington.
“This marks the first known case of HPAI in cattle in Washington state,” state officials said. Since March 2024 dairy cattle herds in 19 states have documented H5N1 infections, including neighboring Idaho.
“Washington State Department of Agriculture conducted on-farm investigations, testing, and gathered additional epidemiological information to better understand this detection and limit further disease spread,” officials said. “The two farms are under quarantine and have employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows.”
Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows.
In the past 30 days four dairy herds have had H5N1 detections, including herds in Kansas and Texas. So far in 2026, US officials have confirmed avian flu in 93 dairy herds, compared to 917 in 2024 and 171 last year.
“We appreciate how difficult this is for our dairy families, farmworkers, and veterinarians that are working hard to keep animals safe and healthy,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD. “The most important thing you can do is implement enhanced biosecurity and report symptoms immediately if animals show signs of illness.”
Unannounced drills to assess healthcare facility readiness to manage infectious disease outbreaks in three areas of the United States revealed variable adherence to containment protocols, according to a new study published in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report .
Using a simulated avian flu scenario involving an A(H5) strain with professional actors as patients, local and national public health authorities conducted 73 drills in 69 emergency departments, urgent care centers, and outpatient clinics in New Jersey, New York, and the US Virgin Islands from January to June 2026. The aim was to assess facilities’ ability to rapidly identify and isolate patients with suspected high-consequence infectious diseases.
“Successive recent outbreaks of viral hemorrhagic fevers, novel coronaviruses (e.g., COVID-19), monkeypox [mpox] virus disease, measles, and avian influenza A(H5) have reinforced the importance of rapidly recognizing and safely managing patients with potentially severe transmissible infections at health care facility points of entry, to protect health care workers, patients, and surrounding communities,” the authors wrote.
Facilities conducted symptom screening in 93.2% of the drills, documented travel history on patient arrival in 79.5%, and asked about exposure to avian flu in 9.6%. In 82.2% of drills during which the patient was appropriately masked, the median time from arrival to masking was two minutes, one minute short of the target.
Findings identified opportunities to support these outpatient settings in implementing more robust screening, isolation and notification processes, and IPC training.
Of 71.2% of drills that included patient isolation, the median time to isolation was 11 minutes, one minute shy of the 10-minute goal. A combination of masking and isolation took place in 60.3% of exercises. Patient actors were identified as being at risk for avian flu in 63.4% of cases.
Infection prevention-and-control (IPC) teams were notified or scheduled to be notified in 54.8% of drills, and staff wore all recommended personal protective equipment (PPE) in just 25.0% but wore none in 5.9%.
“These drills identified needs for health care workers and health care facility staff member training to achieve earlier identification, masking, and isolation of potentially infectious febrile patients,” the researchers wrote. “Findings identified opportunities to support these outpatient settings in implementing more robust screening, isolation and notification processes, and IPC training.”
Russia has yet to confirm what caused the lab worker’s death.
A Danish university has approved a CDC-funded study in African newborns, in which only half of babies will receive the hepatitis B vaccine.
The oral microbiota is significantly less diverse in people with severe persistent symptoms than in those with mild symptoms.
A study in blood cancer patients found that intake of foods with high sugar content was linked to less bacterial diversity in the gut.
No other state has reported that many measles cases in 35 years.
Undercover GAO staff were able to acquire four pieces from the HHS and USDA that experts said could have been resold to countries of concern.
Florida has tracked more than 250 locally acquired dengue cases this year.
The US now has 4,080 confirmed cases, more than a quarter of which are in hard-hit Pennsylvania.
The most recent from the DRC shows 8,665 confirmed and 4,178 deaths, with a case-fatality rate of 48%.
