articles.title_orig: Battleground Republicans break with Trump on key issues in final midterm sprint
articles.title_zh: Battleground Republicans break with Trump on key issues in final midterm sprint
articles.content_orig:
Fox News contributor Byron York discusses President Donald Trump’s midterm strategy and lays out where he believes Republicans should focus their campaigning.
Battleground Republicans are breaking from President Donald Trump with increasing frequency as Election Day draws closer and the party fights to protect its congressional majorities.
With just three weeks until voters head to the polls to decide who controls Congress for the latter half of Trump’s term, some Republicans are putting distance between themselves and Trump as the party faces significant political headwinds.
Veteran GOP strategist Doug Heye told Fox News Digital that such a strategy at this juncture was "not a surprise."
"It happens in midterms when presidents aren’t popular," Heye said. "Add to that the more outlandish things he’s done — often on things that have nothing to do with lowering costs, ending the war with Iran, etc. — this was bound to happen."
TRUMP VANISHES FROM GOP SENATOR'S CAMPAIGN WEBSITE AS POLL NUMBERS PLUNGE WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION
President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Tenn., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
It’s a similar situation to what’s played out with past presidents during a midterm election year, most recently with former President Joe Biden in 2022.
And the Republican National Committee (RNC) is arguing that the party is united behind Trump, while conceding that GOP candidates have individual stakes.
"Unlike the Democrats who are in a full-blown civil war with extremists, Republicans remain united behind the president's agenda of cutting taxes, lowering drug costs and securing our communities. We are laser-focused on winning, and our candidates will run the races necessary to best represent their districts and prevent Democrats from taking control," RNC spokeswoman Natalie Baldessarre said.
And running their own races is what several are notably doing, balancing individuality with their support for Trump and the GOP base.
At least two House Republicans, Reps. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., and Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., have touted conflict with Trump in advertisements.
TRUMP-LINKED SUPER PAC PULLS FUNDING FROM 2 HOUSE REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY
President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he arrives at the White House on Marine One, Sept. 23, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo)
Kiggans is out with a new ad touting herself as "one of the most bipartisan members of Congress," who has taken on her "own party to protect jobs, and working with Democrats to save healthcare." One visual referenced a news article that said, "Kiggans bucks Trump on offshore wind."
Meanwhile, Lawler recently released an advertisement in which he highlighted taking on "the left and the right," followed by a clip of Trump calling him a "pain in the a--" on state and local tax deduction issues.
But for many, like Lawler, it’s a balancing act of trying to keep Trump and the GOP base happy, while courting independent voters.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said, "No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the president understands how to communicate with them."
"President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," Ingle told Fox News Digital.
"The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs," Ingle continued. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction."

articles.title_orig: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
articles.title_zh: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
articles.content_orig:
Drawing on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, a Guardian investigation reveals the murderous cost of our insatiable appetite for cocaine
Read more: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’ Explainer: What is state capture and why does it matter?
As abductions go, few have been more brazen. Alan Jalloh was with two friends outside Goodies supermarket, frantic as usual with late afternoon shoppers. Rush hour in downtown Freetown, Sierra Leone’s capital, was under way with familiar gusto.
A black Toyota Rav4 forced its way through the Peninsula highway traffic. Witnesses describe burly white men leaping out, yanking on balaclavas. Jalloh, 40, seemed to freeze. As did his two friends, one a famous Freetown footballer. All three were dragged into the waiting SUV. None of them have been seen since.
Two days later, on 25 October 2025, another three men disappeared. Within a week, nine people had been seized from the city’s streets, most in broad daylight. They were dismembered, police sources were told. At least one was beheaded. An officer investigating Jalloh’s abduction, says: “They were exterminated to hide the truth.”
No bodies have been found.
Five months after Jalloh disappeared, an ageing cargo ship, the Arconian , left Freetown. By May, it was navigating savage seas 100 miles off the coast of Morocco when Spanish civil guards boarded. Lucas Fernández*, clutching his assault rifle on the ship’s lower deck, stumbled across figures in the Arconian’s darkened cargo hold.
Fernández raised his gun, finger on the trigger. A man pointed an assault rifle back at him. Time stood still. Fernández says the man became agitated, yelling in English, incomprehensible above the storm outside. “It was crazy,” Fernández says.
Within minutes, he and his fellow officers had disarmed six gunmen found hiding in the bowels of the ship. Nearby, were 1,279 bales of cocaine wrapped in plastic; weighing between 30 and 45 tonnes, it is the largest amount of the drug ever seized.
Seventeen days later, the audience at Oxford University rose to applaud the guest speaker. Julius Maada Bio had nailed it once again. His address – eulogising robust leadership – was the latest in a whirlwind year for the president of Sierra Leone.
The chair of Ecowas – the Economic Union of West African States , a region home to more than 400 million people, Bio is among the most influential African voices in the UN. The EU sees Bio as one of its most reliable allies in Africa and has a long history of showering the impoverished country with aid stretching back more than 45 years .
But the most important figure in Sierra Leone is not this ambitious politician, but the man who ordered the abduction of Jalloh; the man responsible for the Arconian’s monumental cocaine stash. A man called Jos Leijdekkers . He also happens to be Bio’s son-in-law.
At 35, Leijdekkers is Europe’s pre-eminent cocaine baron . Intelligence assessments credit the Dutchman with importing volumes vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market. Last year, he halved the drug’s wholesale price. Multiple intelligence sources confirm he has also transformed Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state.
“It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen,” says a western official.
At least 14 people have been killed inside Sierra Leone on Leidjekkers’ orders. High-ranking police are believed to have been murdered on his say-so. Officers have fled the country fearing they will be next.
“If you get in his way, he wipes you out,” says an intelligence source.
Like most, they spoke on condition of anonymity, aware of Leidjekkers’ capacity to reach those who cross him.
Sierra Leone’s fate is a tale of western duplicity. Despite detailed intelligence of the extraordinary volumes of cocaine being exported to Europe , the EU continued to woo Bio and his government. The UN did the same: overlooking its own evidence.
And intelligence sources warn that Leijdekkers’ network is rapidly expanding. “The entire west Africa region is at risk,” says a Dutch official.
Leijdekkers’ prodigious transcontinental network brings deadly violence.
Dozens of his gunmen descended on a sleepy Dutch village last month intent on retribution. A European police source said: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.”
The first recorded sighting of Leijdekkers in west Africa came in October 2022. A six-vehicle convoy thundered down Aberdeen Road, towards Lumley beach, leaving Freetown traffic police baffled. No one had briefed they were expecting VIPs. “‘The convoy was bigger than our president’s,” says one officer.
Unaware of Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker, Freetown police were sufficiently concerned to begin surveillance on the mysterious convoy, which had stopped outside the Sky Bar , a nightlife institution in the city.
At 4am, the group were trailed to a waterfront house near Hamilton beach. There, the covert surveillance team were stunned: revellers included their own bosses.
At the time, western intelligence agencies had no idea of Leijdekkers’ whereabouts. One of Europe’s most wanted men had simply vanished. For years, authorities had tracked his rise in the Dutch underworld, watching how the local hitman from the well-heeled town of Prinsenbeek accrued key contacts for transatlantic cocaine shipments.
When Dutch intelligence traced Leijdekkers to Sierra Leone in 2024, he had created something remarkable: a sprawling cocaine empire from scratch.
“He’s very adept at adaptation, cultivating ties,” says an official. “A new country, but he won over its most influential people.”
That included marrying the president’s daughter, Agnes Bio, and starting a family. Sierra Leone’s top officials partied with the moneyed new guy. Immigration chiefs secured him a diplomatic passport. The person whose job it was to investigate cocaine traffickers became a drinking buddy.
Leijdekkers’ wealth corrupted. According to intelligence, he was generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the running cost of Sierra Leone’s entire state.
Hundreds of people were on his payroll, say sources, including senior military and police figures. But what Leijdekkers coveted most was Freetown’s seaport: the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, perfectly sited between cocaine-producing South America and Europe’s booming markets.
In August 2023, his wife’s uncle, Yankuba Bio, became head of the port. Yankuba Bio denies a close relationship with “any individual called or identified as Jos Leijdekkers”. Sources, though, say port officials on Leijdekkers’s payroll make $2,000 a month – more than 30 times the national average .
In January 2025, the Dutch sent an extradition request to Sierra Leone for the fugitive, who had been sentenced in absentia to more than 100 years in prison for crimes including attempted murder.
Sierra Leone denied knowing the man. For Leijdekkers, it was a defining moment: he had state protection. His confidence culminated in the arrival into Freetown’s port on 18 April of the Arconian, a green cargo vessel the length of a football pitch. Over the next four days, about 30 tonnes of cocaine were hauled onboard, according to western intelligence.
“From experience, the maximum you can hide is eight tonnes. Thirty tonnes says you’re operating in plain sight,” says a UN agent. Yankuba Bio says such claims are “false, completely untrue and without foundation” adding that the port “does not engage in or facilitate the export” of cocaine.
On 26 April, a cryptic tip-off electrified European investigators. An unidentified vessel had left west Africa carrying 18 tonnes of cocaine, the second-largest such cargo identified in Europe.
Within 70 hours, the Arconian had been identified. At 8pm on 1 May, with the vessel pitching in brutal, black seas, Fernández, of Spain’s civil guard central operational unit , was first onboard.

articles.title_orig: Skipping Secularism: 2 Clues from the End of the World
articles.title_zh: Skipping Secularism: 2 Clues from the End of the World
articles.content_orig:
The world is a confusing place right now. We believe that faithful proclamation of the gospel is what our hostile and disoriented world needs. Do you believe that too? Help TGC bring biblical wisdom to the confusing issues across the world by making a gift to our international work.
Maybe it was the whale meat I was eating. Or the earlier round of herring shark. But as I asked questions of my new friends on the Faroe Islands, my view of secularism began to fill up and fill in. They gave me two new clues in my efforts to understand and ultimately reverse the conditions of Western secularism.
When you visit the Faroe Islands, you can’t take your eyes off the scenery—especially on rare days when the sun shines.
As I wrote about after my visit to Copenhagen last year , we can see the conditions that have delivered storm clouds of secularism across much of northern Europe. The combination of Protestantism and established churches has dismantled Christian belief and especially practice in the region.
In this land, the light of gospel radiates more brightly than anywhere else in the Nordic region
The exception can be found on the Faroe Islands, whose windswept fjords feel like the end of world, amid the vast Atlantic Ocean between Iceland and Norway, north of the Shetland and Hebrides isles. In this land where the sun almost never shines (no city in the whole world is gloomier than the Faroese capital, Tórshavn) the light of gospel radiates more brightly than anywhere else in the Nordic region.
Why? I asked my gracious hosts as they fed me from the bounty of the sea, as they drove me through horizontal rains around mountain turns, as they honored their ancestors with the story of their persevering faith.
The first clue came in our visit to Fuglafjørður, situated in the northeast on the island of Eysturoy. From our host we learned about his great-grandfather, the 20th-century Brethren missionary and Bible translator Victor Danielsen.
The statue outside his former church commemorates Danielsen’s most notable accomplishment, the first Bible translated for the common people in Faroese instead of the colonial Danish. Today, the Brethren compose at least 10 percent of the islands’ population of some 55,000, including the 29-year-old prime minister, who was on my flight to Copenhagen. He planned to meet with the Danish king.
The Faroese treasure their independence within the Danish Commonwealth. Not until 1938 did the Faroe Islands secure Danish permission to use Faroese in their churches and schools. It’s no coincidence that Danielsen’s New Testament translation published one year earlier, in 1937 .
Early Brethren missionaries from the United Kingdom saw no spiritual fruit from their labors for two decades. But with Danielsen’s ministry, the Brethren became champions of the ordinary Faroese, who trace ethnic roots to the British Isles, shared colonial identity to Greenland, and remote island affinity to Iceland.
I’ve observed in studies of secularism in the modern West that thriving Christian movements require medium tension with their host cultures. But opposition isn’t sufficient. The Brethren wouldn’t have gained a missionary foothold only by criticizing Lutheran state religion. Resisting secularism requires channeling the aspirations of the people too.
The Brethren set themselves apart with a high view of biblical authority and countercultural holiness, traits that still characterize their followers even as they’ve ascended into the islands’ globally engaged business elite. But they also came to embody native Faroese values and aspirations as a free and independent people, proud of their ancient island culture. In this they resemble the history of Presbyterian missions in Korea as well as the Persian culture that at least last decade held out against Islamic hegemony in Iran.
After preaching Esther 4 in view of the lovely fjord village of Norðragøta, I spoke with Brethren who have earned PhDs in the United Kingdom, opposed abortion and gay marriage in the Faroese Parliament, and traveled the world to represent local business interests (at least 90 percent of the islands’ exports relate to the fishing industry).
For such a remote setting, the high standard of living surprised me. The Faroes’ GDP per capita exceeds Denmark , even if it falls short of the world-leading Norwegians and their vast oil reserves. Many of the homes appeared new, compared to what I’ve seen in other Nordic countries. Over that succulent meal of whale and shark, I learned that the prosperity dates back only about 30 years, and especially in the last 15, due to the success of salmon farming and rising fish prices, following a collapse of the Faroe economy in the 1990s.
Once again, Faroese Christianity bucks the trend, providing the second clue. Economic development is supposed to deliver secularism. That’s the story Denmark and other Nordic countries tell of their “modern breakthrough,” the transition from the backward, rural 19th century to the progressive, urbane 20th.
But what if secularism is less of an economic inevitability and more of a philosophical fad taking root in the developed West roughly between the 1860s and 1960s? And what if lack of economic development during that century shielded some cultures from the full effects of secularism? Even when those cultures catch up, they don’t necessarily descend the whole ladder to secularism.
In this regard, the Faroe Islands could be similar to regions of the United States, especially the Southeast, that developed later and thus far retain much higher rates of Christian belief and observance compared to regions that prospered during that earlier period. And like the Southeast, the Faroe Islands have become a missionary engine, launching gospel workers throughout Europe and even around the world.
Have my new friends in the Faroe Islands helped cracked the code to Christian endurance amid secularism? I wouldn’t put anything past these resilient people tucked inside treeless mountains on the shores of the mighty Atlantic.
What if secularism is less of an economic inevitability and more of a philosophical fad?
Perhaps the period of acute secularism could be skipped, and we’re not waiting for another shoe to drop as the Faroe Islands prosper. Perhaps the Brethren have charted a course for us from the edge of the world. Moderate cultural opposition is necessary but not sufficient. The gospel’s indigenizing principle must also capture the aspirations of people made in the image of God as they enjoy his common grace.
Big breakthroughs can start in small places. Of all people, Christians know that story.

    longings. We want to train Christians—everyone from pastors to parents to
    professors—to boldly share the good news of Jesus Christ in a way that clearly

He hosts the Gospelbound podcast, writes the weekly Unseen Things newsletter, and has written and contributed to many books, including Timothy Keller: His Spiritual and Intellectual Formation and Rediscover Church: Why the Body of Christ Is Essential . He has published with the New York Times and the Washington Post and offered commentary for CNN, Fox News, NPR, BBC, ABC News, and PBS NewsHour . articles.title_orig: In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026
articles.title_zh: In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026
articles.content_orig:
In exactly a month, on November 13, 2026, the world will end. Fittingly, our impending apocalypse falls on Friday the 13th .
At least, that was the prediction made by University of Illinois physicist Heinz von Foerster in a highly cited Science paper published in 1960. Though talks of supposed doomsday have renewed in recent months thanks to hyperbolic anxieties over runaway, sentient artificial intelligence, von Foerster had a much different calamity in mind.
For more than a century, the prevailing fear, dating back to English economist Thomas Malthus who lived between 1766 to 1834, was of a booming population outrunning its food supply. Famine would ensue. But Von Foerster broke from that view. He assumed (correctly, as it turns out) that human ingenuity would keep the world mostly fed. The problem, he argued, was that the population would keep accelerating, toward “infinity.”
In a now infamous quote, von Foerster predicted, “Our great—great—grandchildren will not starve to death,” von Foerster and his co-authors wrote. “They will be squeezed to death.” Homo sapiens’ last gasping breath, they predicted, would peter out in the fall of 2026.
It’s pretty clear that von Foerster’s estimate was dead wrong. Not only is the global population ( around 8.3 billion people ) not expanding near the rate it was when he was writing, but there are actually concerns it’s moving in the opposite direction . In dozens of countries around the world, from South Korea and Japan to much of Western Europe, the concern among demographers has shifted from worries about overpopulation to declining birth rates.
In the United States, President Donald Trump has jumped on the issue, calling himself the “ fertilization president ” offering tax incentives for new families and even exploring medals for women who give birth to six or more children. Joseph Stalin previously championed that last idea.
So how was a prediction so wrong and still so influential? Human population experts speaking with Popular Science say von Foerster and his contemporaries based their prediction on real trends from the past while utterly failing to see the world changing right before their eyes. Though they may have accurately measured growth rates up to that point, that only tells part of the story.
“He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,” Rockefeller University and Columbia University professor and mathematical biologist Joel Cohen tells Popular Science. Cohen has studied human population changes for years and published the influential 1995 book How Many People Can the Earth Support?
“Von Foerster didn’t know at the time, and in fact, nobody knew” that the all-time population growth had already happened, Cohen adds. “The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s.”
Von Foerster and his colleagues published their “Doomsday” paper on November 4, 1960. The dramatic pronouncement hinges on an equation that projects the human population into the future based on past trends.
The team gathered 24 estimates of world population dating back 2,000 years. The key assumption underpinning their logic was that humans differ from other animals because of our unique ability to cooperate and innovate.
Fruit flies in a jar eventually level off as crowding and competition take their toll. Humans, on the other hand, the authors argue, work the other way. The more of us there are, the better we get at cooperating. And the better we get at cooperation, the faster our population grows.
Follow that curve forward, and the population doesn’t just grow; it rockets toward infinity, hitting the so-called mathematical wall on November 13, 2026, give or take five years.
Von Foerster wasn’t alone in sounding the alarm either. Eight years later, biologist Paul R. Ehrlich would publish The Population Bomb , arguably the most influential single text fueling overpopulation fears.
“Both of those guys were right looking backward, but wrong looking forward,” Cohen says.
At a glance, thinking the future will resemble the past seems pretty reasonable. The human population grew steadily but slowly over much of our roughly 300,000 years of humanity. But that changed radically with the onset of globalization, colonization, and the Industrial Revolution.
As Darrell Bricker and John Ibbitson note in their 2020 book Empty Planet: The Shock of Global Population Decline , human population passed the one billion mark somewhere around 1800. That doubled to two billion by 1927. Then doubled again just less than 50 years later in 1974. It would then only take another 13 years to cross the five billion mark. And in 2022, we surpassed eight billion.
That remarkable explosion had many causes, Cohen says, but among the most important was the spread of cheap, calorie-dense crops like potatoes and corn from the Americas.
Crucially, though, humans weren’t necessarily having way more kids. They were just far better at keeping them alive.
“Humanity got better at keeping the people who were born alive through simple, but important innovations like the germ theory of disease, sanitation, nutrition,” University of Texas Associate professor and economic demographer Dean Spears tells Popular Science.
Demographers like Spears study human populations and how they change over time. He published a book on the topic titled After the Spike , earlier this year. Advances in nutrition and medicine “caused early life mortality rates to fall, so more of the humans who were born survived and that caused the population to grow.”
Factoring in longer life expectancy and reductions in child mortality around the world blows a huge hole in Von Foerster’s calculations. Death rates can only fall so far, and once most children survive, families tend to have fewer of them.
The population boom was a one time explosion, not an ever-accelerating loop.
Von Foerster’s assumption of endlessly accelerating growth, Spears says, was “based on a misunderstanding of where population growth comes from.”
Experts specializing in human population studies at the time actually knew that was the case, Spears notes.
Neither von Foerster’s nor Ehrlich (who wrote The Population Bomb) were human population experts. Von Foerster’s background was in physics and philosophy. Ehrlich was a biologist. But they were both great at getting attention.
Indeed, academics at the time reportedly sent flustered letters to the editor at Science , calling the prediction “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd.”
“There was never, even at that time, any reason to think that it would keep growing fast like that.” Spears says. “Paul Ehrlich was a biologist who studied butterflies , not human demography.”
In the later 20th century, population growth actually started declining quite rapidly thanks to a convergence of a variety of factors.
The “Green Revolution” in farming meant that more food could be grown on the same plot of land, which extinguished fears of humanity suddenly starving itself. The first birth control pill , approved by the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) in the U.S. in 1957 , also gave women more autonomy to decide when and how many children to have.
These trends, along with global population shifts away from rural areas and towards more urban areas, would eventually shift concerns away from overpopulation and towards declining birth rates.
Although demographers and policy experts debate how much people should worry about declining birth rates, it is generally agreed that an older population that significantly outnumbers younger people can lead to long-term strains on the country’s economy and social services.
With fewer workers needed in the field, more and more people moved to cities. Historically, families living on farms or agricultural communities tend to have more children than those in urban areas because those children could work the land and, in a purely economic sense, provide more labor and, hopefully, make the family more money.
